rd-school-c5-evs-a.ch3-from-tasting-to-d.title: From Tasting to Digesting
rd-school-c5-evs-a.ch3-from-tasting-to-d.subtitle: How your tongue tastes, why chewing matters, the doctor who peeped into a stomach, and why every child needs good food

sections.md:
Blindfold a friend. Hold their nose. Put a tiny piece of apple on their tongue — then a piece of raw potato. Can they tell which is which? Very often, they can't! Taste and smell work together.

This chapter follows food on its journey:
1. How the tongue senses different tastes
2. Taste and smell together
3. Saliva — the mouth's helper
4. What happens in the stomach (the famous story of Dr Beaumont)
5. Glucose and energy
6. Why some children don't get enough food — and what is being done

**A word of caution:** do the taste activities only with clean, safe food and a clean spoon, with an adult's permission.

check.q: Why is it harder to tell apple from potato when the nose is held?
check.why: Much of what we call flavour comes from smell; blocking the nose makes foods harder to tell apart.

sections.md:
Look at your tongue in a mirror. It is covered with tiny bumps; inside them are **taste buds**. They sense five basic tastes:

| Taste | Example foods |
|---|---|
| Sweet | jaggery, sugar, ripe banana |
| Salty | salt, chips, namkeen |
| Sour | tamarind, lemon, raw mango |
| Bitter | karela (bitter gourd), neem, coffee |
| Umami (savoury) | tomato, mushrooms, cheese |

**Activity (from the chapter idea):** Put a little sugar, then salt, then lemon juice, then a bit of neem or bitter gourd on different parts of your tongue (rinse between each). Note what you feel.

**Old idea, new facts:** Many old books drew a *tongue map* with sweet only at the tip and bitter at the back. Scientists now know that **all parts of the tongue can sense all tastes**; some areas may be a little more sensitive. A dry tongue tastes poorly — wetness (saliva) is needed to dissolve food so taste buds can sense it.

sections.h: Chew, chew, chew — saliva at work
sections.md:
**Activity:** Take a small piece of roti or bread and chew it slowly for a long time — 30 times or more. What happens? It starts to taste **slightly sweet**!

Why? Your mouth makes **saliva** (spit). Saliva:
- makes food wet and soft so it can be swallowed,
- helps us taste,
- contains a substance that begins breaking down **starch** (in roti, rice, potato) into **sugar**.

We make saliva when we see, smell or even *think* of tasty food — your mouth may be watering right now if you're thinking of hot pakoras on a rainy day!

**Chewing** breaks food into small bits. That's why elders say *chew your food well* — it makes the stomach's work easier.

**After swallowing**, food travels down the **food pipe (oesophagus)** to the stomach. Even if you stand on your head, food goes to the stomach — muscles push it along.

check.q: Why does roti taste sweet after long chewing?
check.why: Saliva starts breaking down starch into sugar, which tastes sweet.

sections.h: A window into the stomach — Dr Beaumont's story
sections.md:
In 1822, in North America, a young man called **Alexis St. Martin** was accidentally shot in the stomach. A doctor, **William Beaumont**, treated him. Alexis survived, but the wound healed in a strange way — it left a small **opening** from the outside of his body into his stomach.

Dr Beaumont realised this was a rare chance to learn how the stomach works. Over several years, with Alexis's help, he:
- tied small pieces of food to a thread and put them into the stomach through the opening, pulling them out after some hours to see how much had been digested;
- took out some of the stomach's juices and saw that they could break down food even outside the body, in a bottle;
- noticed that the stomach **churns** food and that worry or anger affected digestion.

He learned that the stomach makes **digestive juices** (including an acid) that break food into simpler forms. Digestion is a mix of **churning** (physical) and **juices** (chemical).

From the stomach, food moves to the **small intestine**, where digestion finishes and nutrients pass into the blood. Undigested parts go to the **large intestine** and leave the body as waste.

options: It makes juices that break down food and churns it
It sends food to the lungs
check.why: He found the stomach churns food and releases digestive juices that break it down.

sections.md:
Have you seen someone in a hospital with a bottle and tube attached to the arm? That is often a **glucose drip**. When a person is very weak — for example after loose motions (diarrhoea) or when they cannot eat — doctors give glucose straight into the blood.

**Glucose** is a simple sugar. Our body breaks down much of our food into glucose, and our cells use it for **energy**. Because glucose is already simple, the body doesn't need to digest it, so it gives energy quickly.

**Diarrhoea and ORS:** When we lose a lot of water through loose motions, the body becomes **dehydrated**. **ORS** (oral rehydration solution) puts back water, salt and sugar. Packet ORS from a chemist or health centre, mixed exactly as written on the packet, is best. Health workers also teach a home sugar-salt solution (for 1 litre of clean, boiled and cooled water, the commonly taught measure is 6 level teaspoons of sugar and half a level teaspoon of salt) — an adult should make it. *Always see a doctor if a child has diarrhoea for long or seems very weak.*

check.q: Why does a glucose drip give quick energy?
options: Glucose is already simple and needs no digestion
check.why: Glucose is a simple sugar the cells can use straight away for energy.

sections.h: Food for all — hunger and the mid-day meal
sections.md:
The chapter also asks: *do all children get enough to eat?* Many children in India and around the world still do not. When children don't get enough good food for a long time they may become **weak**, fall ill often, grow slowly, and find it hard to study. Not having enough **iron** in food can cause **anaemia** — tiredness and pale skin.

To help, many states began serving a free cooked **mid-day meal** in government schools, and in 2001 the Supreme Court ordered it across India. It is now called **PM POSHAN**. A hot meal of dal, rice, vegetables or roti keeps children healthy and helps more children come to school.

**Balanced diet:** Eat a mix of grains (energy), dal, milk, eggs or pulses (body-building), fruit and vegetables (protection), and drink clean water.

> Did you know? Your stomach can stretch to hold more than a litre of food, and the small intestine of an adult is about 6–7 metres long!

check.q: Lack of iron in food can cause…
check.why: Iron is needed to make healthy blood; too little iron leads to anaemia.

All parts of the tongue can sense all tastes.
Smell and taste work together to give flavour.
Saliva wets food and begins turning starch into sugar.

Food goes down the food pipe to the stomach, pushed by muscles.

The stomach churns food and adds digestive juices.

Glucose is a simple sugar that gives quick energy.

rd-school-c5-evs-a.ch4-mangoes-round-the.title: Mangoes Round the Year
rd-school-c5-evs-a.ch4-mangoes-round-the.subtitle: Why food spoils, the fuzzy fungus on old bread, and how families keep mangoes for months as aam papad and pickle

sections.md:
Mango season in India is short — roughly April to July. Yet in December your grandmother might open a jar of *aam ka achaar* or hand you a strip of chewy, sweet **aam papad**. How did summer's mangoes survive till winter?

This chapter is about **food spoiling and food saving**:
1. How we know food has gone bad
2. Why food spoils — the fungus-on-bread experiment
3. Which foods spoil fast and which last long
4. Ways of preserving food at home
5. The story of making aam papad
6. Saving food in big ways — and not wasting it

check.q: About when is mango season in most of India?
check.why: Most Indian mangoes ripen in the hot months, roughly April to July.

sections.h: How do we know food has spoiled?
sections.md:
Use your senses — carefully!

- **Smell:** sour or bad smell (spoilt milk, dal left out on a hot day)
- **Look:** changed colour, white/green/black fuzzy patches, slime
- **Taste:** sour or strange (only a tiny bit, and never if it looks or smells bad)
- **Touch:** sticky, slimy or too soft (an over-ripe tomato)

**Never eat spoiled food** — it can cause stomach pain, vomiting and loose motions (food poisoning).

**Which spoil fast?** Cooked rice and dal, milk, paneer, cut fruit — especially in hot, humid weather. **Which last longer?** Dry grains (rice, wheat, dal), whole spices, jaggery, sugar, salt — because they have very little water.

check.q: Why do dry grains last longer than cooked rice?
options: They have very little water, so germs can't grow easily
check.why: Tiny living things that spoil food need water; dry grains have very little, so they keep longer.

sections.h: The bread experiment — meet the fungus
sections.md:
**Activity:** Take a piece of bread or roti. Sprinkle a few drops of water on it and keep it in a closed box in a warm place. Look at it every day for a week (don't touch or smell closely — use a hand lens if you have one). Record what you see:

| Day | What we see |
|---|---|
| 1–2 | no change, a bit soft |
| 3 | tiny white spots |
| 4–5 | spots spread, become fluffy, grey-green or black |
| 6–7 | bread covered with fuzzy patches, bad smell |

The fuzzy growth is a **fungus** (mould). Fungi are tiny living things. Their **spores** float in the air all the time — invisible! When they land on food that is **moist and warm**, they grow and spoil it.

**Try it:** Keep one piece dry, one wet, one in the fridge. Which gets fungus first? Usually the **wet, warm** one. Cold and dryness slow fungus down.

sections.h: Ways to keep food from spoiling
sections.md:
People have found many clever ways to **preserve** food — all work by stopping germs and fungi from growing.

| Method | How it works | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Drying in the sun | removes water | papad, vadi, dried chillies, raw-mango *amchur*, fish |
| Salt | draws out water; germs can't live | pickles, salted fish, lemon in salt |
| Sugar / jaggery | thick sugar stops germs | murabba, jam, aam papad |
| Oil | covers food, keeps air out | mango/lime pickles |
| Vinegar | sour; germs dislike it | onion, chilli pickles |
| Cold | slows germs | refrigerator, matka for water |
| Boiling | kills germs | boiling milk twice a day |
| Airtight cans/packets | no air or germs get in | packed juices, tinned food |

When you buy packaged food, read the **date of manufacture** and **best before/expiry** date on the pack.

check.q: How does salt help preserve pickles?
options: It draws out water so germs can't grow
check.why: Salt pulls water out of food and germs, so they cannot grow and spoil it.

sections.h: Making aam papad — a family story
sections.md:
It is a scorching June morning in a village near Lucknow. Aapa (elder sister) calls the children: *"Come — today we make aam papad!"*

1. **Choose:** ripe, sweet, juicy mangoes are washed.
2. **Pulp:** the mangoes are peeled and squeezed; the pulp is strained through a cloth so no fibres remain.
3. **Sweeten:** jaggery or sugar is mixed in (some add a pinch of salt or cardamom).
4. **Spread:** a thin layer of pulp is spread on a clean, oiled plate, mat or cloth.
5. **Dry:** the plates are kept in hot sun for several days. A net or cloth is put on top to keep away flies, dust and birds; they are taken in at night.
6. **Layer:** when one layer is dry, another is spread on top — again and again until it is thick.
7. **Cut and store:** it is cut into pieces and stored in an airtight jar.

**Why does it last?** The sun dries out the water, and the sugar stops germs. Together they keep mangoes 'round the year'.

**Also:** raw mangoes become *amchur* (dried mango powder), *aam panna* concentrate and many pickles — each region has its own.

options: To keep away flies, dust and birds
check.why: The net keeps it clean and safe from insects and birds while it dries.

sections.h: Food that travels, and food we waste
sections.md:
Today trucks with **cold storage** and big warehouses help fruits and grain travel long distances — mangoes from Ratnagiri reach Delhi, apples from Himachal reach Chennai. Grain is kept in government godowns. But if storage is poor, rain, rats and fungus can spoil huge amounts.

At home and at weddings, a lot of cooked food is thrown away. Ideas to **reduce waste**:
- Cook and serve only what is needed; take small helpings.
- Store leftovers covered and cool; use them soon.
- Share extra food with neighbours or food banks.
- Compost peels and scraps.

> Did you know? Some pickles in Indian homes stay good for over a year because of salt, oil and spices — that's preservation science passed down for generations!

check.q: Which is a good way to reduce food waste at a feast?
options: Take small helpings and go back if needed
check.why: Taking small helpings means less food left on plates and thrown away.

summary: Mango season is short, but preserved mangoes last all year.
Spoiled food shows changes in smell, look, taste and touch.
Never eat spoiled food — it causes food poisoning.
Food with more water (cooked rice, milk) spoils faster than dry grains.
Fungus (mould) grows from tiny spores in the air.
Fungus grows best where it is moist and warm.
Food is preserved by drying, salt, sugar, oil, vinegar, cold, boiling and airtight packing.
Packets show manufacture and expiry dates.
Aam papad: mango pulp + sugar, spread thin and sun-dried layer by layer.
Sun removes water and sugar stops germs.
Cold storage helps food travel; poor storage wastes grain.
We can reduce waste by cooking and serving only what is needed.

sections.md:
The chapter asks you to try a simple experiment. Take a slice of bread, sprinkle a few drops of water on it, and keep it in a closed box in a warm corner. Look at it every day for a week and fill a table like the one below.

After two or three days you see tiny white or greenish-black spots. With a magnifying glass they look like fine threads or cotton — this is **fungus (mould)**. It grows fastest when there is **moisture, warmth and air**. A dry slice kept in a fridge spoils much more slowly.

**Safety:** never smell mould closely or eat it, and wash your hands after the activity.

sections.h: How do we know food has spoilt?
sections.md:
Our senses are detectives:
- **Look** — changed colour, spots, fungus.
- **Smell** — sour or rotten smell.
- **Taste** — sour or strange taste (never test doubtful food!).
- **Touch** — slimy or sticky.

Different foods last for different times. Cooked dal or rice may spoil in a day in summer; bread in a few days; potatoes and onions for weeks; pickles, jam and papad for months. Seasons matter too — food spoils faster in hot, humid monsoon weather.

Families across India use many methods, often without a fridge:

| Method | Example |
|---|---|
| Drying in the sun | aam papad, papad, dried red chillies, sukha mewa |
| Salt and oil | mango and lemon pickles |
| Sugar | jam, murabba, aam ka chunda |
| Cold | refrigerator, matka for water |
| Boiling | milk boiled twice a day |
| Airtight jars | keeping biscuits crisp |

Salt and sugar pull water out of the food, so germs cannot grow. Drying removes water directly. That is why aam papad made in summer can be enjoyed in winter — mangoes *round the year*!

**Did you know?** Packets carry a 'best before' or expiry date. Always check it before buying.

check.q: Why does salt help a pickle last long?
options: It removes water so germs can't grow
check.why: Salt draws water out of food, and without water germs and mould cannot multiply.

summary: Mould is a fungus that grows on damp, warm food.

Different foods last different lengths of time.

Drying, salting, sugar, cold and boiling preserve food.
Aam papad is mango pulp dried in the sun.
Check expiry dates on packets.

rd-school-c5-evs-a.ch5-seeds-and-seeds.title: Seeds and Seeds
rd-school-c5-evs-a.ch5-seeds-and-seeds.subtitle: Sprouting moong, what a seed needs, seeds that fly, float, hitch rides and burst — and plants that travelled to India from far away

sections.h: A seed is a baby plant in a lunch box
sections.md:
Soak a few moong beans overnight. In the morning they are fat; in a day or two, tiny white tails pop out. In a week, green leaves! Where was that plant hiding? Inside the seed, all along — a **baby plant (embryo)** packed with its own **food store**, wrapped in a protective **seed coat**, like a lunch box.

In this chapter:
1. Sprouting seeds at home
2. What seeds need to grow — an experiment
3. Looking inside a seed
4. How seeds travel far from the parent plant
5. Plants that came to India from other lands
6. Seeds in our kitchen and farms

check.q: What does the seed coat do?
check.why: The seed coat is a protective cover around the embryo and its food store.

sections.md:
**Activity:**
1. Soak a handful of moong or chana in water overnight.
2. Drain the water and wrap the seeds in a wet cotton cloth.
3. Keep the bundle in a warm place; sprinkle water twice a day.
4. Look every day and draw what you see.

| Day | What happens |
|---|---|
| 1 | seeds swell, skin wrinkles |
| 2 | a tiny white root (radicle) peeps out |
| 3–4 | root grows longer, hair-like roots appear |
| 5–7 | a shoot with small leaves comes up |

The first part to come out is the **root**, which grows **down**; the shoot grows **up** towards light. Sprouts are also a healthy food — many families eat sprouted moong with lemon, onion and tomato.

fig.alt: A seed in soil sends a root down and a shoot with two leaves up.

check.q: Which part comes out of a sprouting seed first?
check.why: The root (radicle) emerges first and grows downward to anchor the seedling and absorb water.

sections.h: What do seeds need to sprout? — an experiment
sections.md:
Take four small bowls with a few soaked moong in each:

| Bowl | Condition | Result after 3–4 days |
|---|---|---|
| A | dry cotton, no water | no sprouting |
| B | wet cotton, warm room | sprouts well |
| C | seeds completely under boiled-and-cooled water (no air) | little or no sprouting |
| D | wet cotton, in the fridge (cold) | very slow or none |

**Conclusion:** Seeds need **water, air and warmth** to sprout. Interestingly, most seeds **don't need sunlight or soil to sprout**, because they have their own stored food. But once the leaves come out, the young plant needs **sunlight** to make food, and soil for minerals.

**Fair test:** change only *one* thing in each bowl, keep everything else the same, so you know what made the difference.

check.q: Which three things do most seeds need to sprout?
check.why: Bowls without water, without air, or kept cold did not sprout — so seeds need water, air and warmth.

sections.md:
Soak a chana or rajma seed overnight and gently peel the skin. It splits into **two halves** — these are **cotyledons** (seed leaves), full of stored food. Between them you'll see a tiny root and shoot — the **embryo**.

Seeds with two halves (chana, moong, rajma, peanut) are called **dicots**; seeds that don't split (maize, wheat, rice) are **monocots**.

**How many seeds in a fruit?** Count! A mango has 1, a litchi 1, a lady's finger (bhindi) dozens, a papaya or watermelon hundreds, a guava many tiny ones. Some fruits like bananas we grow from cuttings/suckers — their tiny seeds don't grow.

**Seeds of different shapes and sizes:** mustard (tiny, round), rajma (kidney-shaped), coconut (huge — one of the biggest seeds), the double coconut (coco de mer) the largest seed in the world.

check.q: What are the two halves of a chana seed called?
check.why: The two halves are cotyledons, seed leaves that store food for the baby plant.

sections.md:
If every seed fell just below its mother tree, the seedlings would fight for light, water and space. So plants have clever ways to send seeds far away — **seed dispersal**:

| How | Seed feature | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Wind | light, with wings or hairs | madar (aak), cotton, drumstick, maple-like *sal* seeds, dandelion |
| Water | light, waterproof, can float | coconut, lotus |
| Animals (eaten) | tasty fruit; seed passes out unharmed | guava, ber, tomato, mango |
| Animals (hitch-hike) | hooks or spines that stick | *gokhru* (puncture vine), grass burrs, chirchita |
| Bursting | pod dries and pops | balsam, pea, lady's finger, castor |
| People | we carry and sow them | wheat, rice, vegetables |

A coconut can float in the sea for weeks and grow on a faraway beach — that's why coconut palms line coasts.

check.q: How does a coconut seed usually travel to new places?
check.why: Coconuts are light and waterproof, so they float on sea water to far-off shores.

sections.h: Plants that came to India from far away
sections.md:
Many foods we think of as completely Indian actually came from other continents, mostly in the last 500 years, brought by traders and travellers (especially the Portuguese, from the 1500s):

| Plant | Came from |
|---|---|
| Chilli (mirch) | South & Central America |
| Tomato | South America |
| Potato | South America (Andes) |
| Maize (makka) | Central America (Mexico) |
| Groundnut (peanut) | South America |
| Cashew | Brazil |
| Papaya | Central America |
| Pineapple | South America |

Before chillies came, Indian food got its heat from **black pepper** and **long pepper** — spices that grew here and were traded across the world.

And India gave the world many plants too — **mango, sugarcane, black pepper, cotton, and many kinds of rice**.

**Saving seeds:** Farmers traditionally saved the best seeds from each harvest. Seed banks today protect thousands of crop varieties so they are not lost.

check.q: Which of these came to India from South America?
check.why: The potato was first grown in the Andes mountains of South America and reached India a few centuries ago.

sections.h: Seeds in the kitchen and the field
sections.md:
Look in your kitchen: **dals and pulses** (moong, masoor, chana, rajma), **grains** (rice, wheat, jowar, bajra, ragi), **spices** (jeera, rai/mustard, methi, saunf, dhaniya, ajwain), **oils** from seeds (mustard, groundnut, sesame, coconut). Seeds feed the whole country!

**On the farm**, seeds are sown by hand broadcasting, in rows with a seed drill, or rice is first grown in a nursery and then transplanted.

> Did you know? Some lotus seeds found in an old lake bed in China sprouted after more than 1,000 years! Seeds can wait a very long time for the right conditions.

check.q: Which of these is a spice made of seeds?
check.why: Jeera is the dried seed of the cumin plant; turmeric and ginger are underground stems.

summary: A seed has a seed coat, stored food and a baby plant (embryo).
Soaked moong and chana sprout in a few days.
The root comes out first and grows down; the shoot grows up.
Seeds need water, air and warmth to sprout.
Most seeds do not need soil or sunlight to sprout, but the young plant needs light to make food.
Change only one thing at a time in a fair test.
Chana and rajma split into two cotyledons (dicots); maize and wheat don't (monocots).
Seeds spread by wind, water, animals, bursting and people.
Spreading seeds avoids crowding under the parent plant.
Chilli, tomato, potato, maize, groundnut and cashew came to India from the Americas.
India gave the world mango, sugarcane, black pepper and cotton.
Our kitchens are full of seeds: dals, grains, spices and oils.
practice: Write the steps for sprouting moong and draw what happens each day.
Design an experiment to show seeds need water to sprout.
Why do most seeds not need sunlight to sprout?
Name two seeds spread by wind, two by water and two by animals.
How does a burr (gokhru) travel? Draw it.
List five plants that came to India from other countries.
Collect ten seeds from your kitchen and group them as dal, grain, spice or oilseed.
Why is it good for a plant that its seeds travel far?

rd-school-c5-evs-a.ch5-seeds-and-seeds-2.title: Seeds and Seeds (part 2)
rd-school-c5-evs-a.ch5-seeds-and-seeds-2.subtitle: Sprouting at home, how seeds travel, and plants that came from far away

sections.md:
Soak a handful of moong, chana or rajma in water overnight. Next morning drain them and tie them in a wet cloth. Keep sprinkling water. In one or two days a tiny white **root** peeps out, and soon a small green **shoot**.

Compare: put some seeds in a dry bowl, some in water all the time, and some on wet cotton. Usually only the seeds that get **water and air** sprout well. Seeds kept dry stay asleep; seeds drowned for days may rot.

Sprouts are tasty and healthy — many homes eat sprouted moong with lemon and salt.

check.q: What do most seeds need to sprout?
check.why: Water wakes the seed up and air lets it breathe, so seeds with both sprout best.

sections.md:
A plant cannot walk, yet its seeds spread far. The chapter shows many ways:
- **Wind:** light, winged or hairy seeds — cotton, aak (madar), drumstick, maple.
- **Water:** coconuts float across seas.
- **Animals:** sticky or hooked seeds (chirchita, gokhru) cling to fur and clothes; birds eat fruits and drop seeds far away.
- **Bursting:** pods of balsam, beans and okra (bhindi) dry and burst, flinging seeds.
- **People:** we carry seeds when we trade and travel.

Spreading out helps young plants get their own space, light and water.

sections.md:
Many foods we think of as Indian came from other lands hundreds of years ago, mostly with traders. **Potato, tomato, chilli, maize, groundnut and papaya** came from the Americas (brought by the Portuguese and others). Tea was grown widely in India by the British. In return, plants like mango, black pepper and sugarcane spread from Asia to the world.

**Did you know?** Before chillies arrived, Indian food got its heat from black pepper and long pepper!

check.q: Which of these came to India from the Americas?
check.why: Chilli plants were brought from the Americas by traders a few hundred years ago.

summary: Seeds sprout with water and air; first a root, then a shoot.
Seeds spread by wind, water, animals, bursting and people.
Light, hairy seeds fly; coconuts float; hooked seeds stick.
Spreading helps plants get space and light.
Potato, tomato, chilli and maize came from the Americas.

rd-school-c5-evs-a.ch6-every-drop-counts.title: Every Drop Counts
rd-school-c5-evs-a.ch6-every-drop-counts.subtitle: In a desert that gets little rain, how did people build lakes, wells and stepwells that lasted centuries?

sections.md:
Imagine standing in **Jaisalmer**, a golden city in the Thar desert of Rajasthan, where rain may fall on only a few days a year. And yet, near the city, there is a large lake with stone steps, temples and carved gateways: **Gadisar (Gharsisar) Lake**. It was built in the 14th century by Maharawal Gharsi, so that rainwater flowing from the land around could be **collected and saved**.

The chapter opens with a visitor's description of this lake: wide stone ghats going down to the water, small temples and pavilions around it, and a beautiful gateway. For hundreds of years the people of Jaisalmer drew water from this lake. Everyone, rich or poor, shared in looking after it. When the lake needed cleaning, the whole town came to help, and the king himself is said to have joined.

The chapter asks big questions: **How did people get water in places where it hardly rains? Who looked after the water? Who owned it?** And what can we learn from them today?

> **Did you know?** The Thar desert gets very little rain in a year — far less than Mumbai or Kolkata get in a single monsoon month.

sections.h: Where does it rain how much?
sections.md:
The textbook shows a **rainfall map of India**. Different colours show how much rain each region gets in a year.

- The **north-east** (Meghalaya — Cherrapunji and Mawsynram) and the **west coast** (Konkan, Kerala) get the **most** rain.
- Western **Rajasthan** (Jaisalmer, Barmer, Bikaner) and parts of Ladakh get the **least**.
- Most of the plains get a medium amount, mostly in the **monsoon months** from June to September.

Activity idea: find your own city or village on the map. Does it get a lot of rain or little? Ask the elders at home: Has the rain changed since they were children? Where did their family get water from when they were young — a well, a river, a pond, a hand pump or a tap?

Even places with heavy rain can run short of water if the rain simply runs away into rivers and the sea. So the trick is not only *how much* rain falls, but *how well* we **catch and store** it.

check.q: Which part of India gets the least rain?
check.why: Western Rajasthan, in the Thar desert, receives the least rainfall in India, so people there learnt to save every drop.

sections.md:
The secret of the desert people was simple: **every drop of rain is precious, so catch it where it falls**. This is called **rainwater harvesting**.

- **Kunds / tankas** — round underground tanks built in courtyards or open land. The ground around slopes towards the tank, and rain flows in through small holes. The top is covered (often with a dome) to keep water clean and cool.
- **Rooftop collection** — rain falling on flat roofs is led by pipes into tanks below the house.
- **Johads** — small mud walls (check dams) built across slopes to stop running rainwater so it soaks into the ground and fills wells.
- **Lakes and tanks** — like Gadisar, built where water from a large area would flow.
- **Kuis** — narrow, deep wells that collect water seeping through the sand.

The area from which rain flows into a tank is called its **catchment area**. People kept the catchment clean: no one was allowed to walk on it with shoes or dirty it.

keyTerms: Rainwater harvesting — collecting and storing rain
Kund/tanka — covered underground water tank
Johad — small earthen check dam
Catchment — land from which rain flows into a tank

check.q: What is a kund?
options: A covered underground tank for rainwater
check.why: A kund is a covered underground tank into which rainwater flows from sloping ground around it.

sections.md:
In Rajasthan and Gujarat you can still see **stepwells**, called **baoli** or **bawdi** (and *vav* in Gujarati). Long flights of stone steps lead down many storeys to the water, which stays cool even in summer. As the water level fell in the dry months, people simply walked further down the steps.

- **Chand Baori** in Abhaneri, Rajasthan, is one of the deepest and most beautiful — about 3,500 narrow steps in a zigzag pattern going down around 13 storeys. It was first built over 1,000 years ago.
- **Rani ki Vav** in Patan, Gujarat, is covered with carved stone figures and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. (Its picture is on the ₹100 note issued in 2018!)

Stepwells were also places to rest and meet. Travellers stopped there; women gathered to fetch water and talk. Rich traders and queens often paid to build them as a gift to the public.

When water started coming through **taps and pipes**, many stepwells and tanks were forgotten. They filled with garbage and some dried up. Today, many towns are cleaning them again.

check.q: Which famous stepwell appears on the ₹100 note?
check.why: Rani ki Vav in Patan, Gujarat, is shown on the ₹100 note issued from 2018.

sections.h: Who looked after the water? Then and now
sections.md:
The chapter also makes us think about **who controls water**. In old times, lakes, tanks and wells were looked after by the **community**. Each family helped dig and clean them, and there were rules: no bathing animals in the drinking tank, no dirty water flowing into the catchment.

During **British rule**, things changed. The government took charge of many water sources and forests; people's own say in caring for them became smaller. Over time, many people began to feel that water was 'someone else's job'.

Today water comes to many homes through **pipes from a dam or a river** far away, managed by the city corporation or the Jal Board. Families get a **water bill**. Some people get plenty, while others — often poorer settlements — get very little and must stand in long queues at a single tap or wait for a **tanker**.

Think and discuss:
- Is it fair if some houses have big tanks and gardens while others have no water to drink?
- Who should decide how water is shared?
- Should water be free for everyone, or should everyone pay something?

There is no single right answer; the chapter wants you to think about **fairness**.

check.q: In old times, who usually cared for village tanks and lakes?
check.why: Traditional lakes and tanks were dug, cleaned and protected by the community, with shared rules for their use.

sections.md:
In the **Alwar** district of Rajasthan, rivers had dried up and villagers were leaving for cities. In the 1980s, **Rajendra Singh** and his group *Tarun Bharat Sangh* worked with villagers to **rebuild old johads**. Thousands of small check dams were built by the people themselves, with their own labour.

Rainwater now stopped and soaked into the ground. Wells filled up again. After some years, rivers that had been dry, such as the **Arvari**, began to flow again! Farming returned, cattle had grass, and families came back. Rajendra Singh is often called the **'Waterman of India'**; in 2015 he received the Stockholm Water Prize.

This shows something important: **communities working together** can heal their land and water.

Many Indian cities face water shortage in summer. People wait for **tankers**, store water in buckets and drums, or buy bottled water. Some families get water from taps for only an hour a day.

Why? Cities are growing, **groundwater** is pumped out faster than rain fills it back, and old lakes have been filled in to build houses and roads. Cement and tar stop rain soaking into the ground.

What can we do?

1. **Harvest rain** from rooftops — many cities now require it for new buildings.
2. **Fix leaking taps.** A tap dripping once a second can waste thousands of litres a year.
3. **Use a bucket, not a shower** or running hose.
4. **Reuse water** — water from washing vegetables can water plants.
5. **Keep lakes and wells clean.**

Activity: keep a **water diary** for one day. Note how many buckets your family uses for drinking, cooking, bathing, washing clothes and cleaning. Where could you save?

head: Old ways
New ways
rows: Government and citizens share the job
fig.caption: Old wisdom, new tools.

check.q: Which habit saves the most water at home?
options: Using a bucket instead of a hose to wash a car
Watering plants at noon with a hose
check.why: A bucket uses only the water needed, while a running hose wastes many litres.

parts.md: Every summer Tara visited her Dadi in a village near Barmer. In the courtyard sat a white, dome-topped kund. 'Our water bank,' Dadi called it. In July, when dark clouds finally rolled in, the whole family swept the courtyard clean so that only clear rain would run into the tank.

That night it poured. Tara lay awake listening to water gurgling through the little holes into the kund. In the morning Dadi lowered a bucket and the water came up cool and sweet. 'This will last us till Diwali if we are careful,' she said.

Back in Jaipur, Tara saw water running from a tap no one had closed. She closed it, then told her school about Dadi's kund. That year her class helped set up a rooftop rain tank for the school garden. They called it 'Dadi's Bank'.

summary: In dry places like the Thar desert, every drop of rain is precious.
Gadisar (Gharsisar) Lake in Jaisalmer was built in the 14th century to store rainwater.
A rainfall map shows Meghalaya and the west coast get most rain; western Rajasthan least.
Rainwater harvesting means collecting and storing rain.
Kunds/tankas are covered underground tanks fed by sloping ground.
Johads are small check dams that help water soak into the ground.
The catchment area is the land from which rain flows into a tank.
Stepwells (baoli, vav) like Chand Baori and Rani ki Vav store water deep and cool.
Communities once cared for water; under British rule and later, control moved to governments.
Water is not shared equally today — some get plenty, some queue at tankers.
Rajendra Singh and villagers revived johads in Alwar; the Arvari river flowed again.
Saving water: harvest rain, fix leaks, use buckets, reuse water.
practice: Why did people of Jaisalmer build Gadisar Lake?
Look at a rainfall map: name two places with high rain and two with low rain.
How does a kund collect water? Draw and label it.
What is a johad? How does it help wells?
Write about one stepwell you have read about.
Who looked after water sources in old times? How has this changed?
Is water shared fairly in your area? Give reasons.
How did the Arvari river start flowing again?
Why do many cities run short of water in summer?
Keep a one-day water diary and suggest three ways to save water.

rd-school-c5-evs-b.ch10-walls-tell-stori.title: Walls Tell Stories
rd-school-c5-evs-b.ch10-walls-tell-stori.subtitle: A clap at the gate heard at the top of a hill — what secrets do the walls of Golconda Fort keep?

sections.h: A clap that travels up a hill
sections.md:
A guide stands under a huge domed gateway and claps once. Far above, at the very top of the hill, someone hears it clearly! Visitors gasp. This is **Golconda Fort**, near **Hyderabad** in Telangana, and the chapter begins with exactly this kind of visit.

The guide explains: hundreds of years ago, if an enemy came to the main gate, a guard could clap or call out here, and the sound would carry all the way up to the king's palace on the hilltop. It was an early **alarm system** — made only with clever design of domes and walls.

In this chapter we follow a family on a tour of the fort and learn how walls, gates, cannons, pipes and broken pieces of pottery can **tell us stories** about people who lived long ago.

> **Think:** Have you visited a fort or palace? What did you notice first — the walls, the gates or the view?

Golconda began as a mud fort. It grew into a mighty stone fort under the **Qutb Shahi** kings, who ruled the region for about 170 years (from the early 1500s to 1687). They made it bigger, with thick walls and many gates.

- The fort had **three lines of walls**, one inside the other. The outer wall ran for many kilometres around the whole town.
- The walls had **87 bastions** (round towers) where guards and cannons stood.
- There were **eight main gates**. The main entrance is the **Fateh Darwaza** (Victory Gate). Its huge wooden doors were studded with long iron **spikes** so that war elephants could not push them open.
- Inside lived not only the king but soldiers, traders, craftsmen and ordinary families — Golconda was almost a city.

In **1687** the Mughal emperor **Aurangzeb** surrounded the fort. The siege lasted about eight months. Historians say the fort fell only when someone inside opened a gate for the Mughal army.

fig.caption: Three rings of walls climb the hill; a clap at the domed gate spreads up to the palace.
fig.alt: Hill fort with three walls and sound rings spreading from the gate to the top.

check.q: Why did the Fateh Darwaza doors have iron spikes?
options: To stop elephants pushing the doors
check.why: Sharp iron spikes stopped enemy war elephants from ramming the doors open.

sections.h: Cannons, ramps and a clever water system
sections.md:
The family sees an old **cannon** on a wall. Cannons were heavy, so how did soldiers move them up? Along gentle **ramps** and slopes instead of steps, pulled by animals and people.

The guide also points out something surprising: **clay pipes** and water channels inside the walls. Water was lifted from tanks below using **Persian wheels** (wheels with pots, turned by bullocks) and then carried through pipes to the palaces and gardens high up, even to fountains! There were baths, store rooms and stables too.

This tells us that the builders understood **engineering**: how to carry water uphill, how to make sound travel, and how to keep cool in the hot Deccan summer with thick walls and high ceilings.
keyTerms: Fort — strong walled place for defence
Bastion — round tower jutting from a wall
Siege — surrounding a fort so no one can go in or out
Persian wheel — wheel with pots to lift water

check.q: How was water carried up to the palace?
options: Lifted by Persian wheels and sent through clay pipes
It rained only on the palace
check.why: Persian wheels lifted water into channels and clay pipes that took it up to the hilltop buildings.

sections.md:
Golconda was famous all over the world for its **diamonds**. They came from mines near the **Krishna river**, such as **Kollur**, and traders brought them to the Golconda market to be cut and sold. Travellers from Europe wrote about the busy diamond trade.

The famous **Koh-i-Noor** diamond is believed to have come from the Golconda region. After passing through the hands of many rulers, it is today part of the British Crown Jewels in London.

> **Did you know?** For a long time, 'Golconda' was used in English to mean 'a source of great riches'.

sections.h: How do we know about the past?
sections.md:
How do people today know what happened in a fort hundreds of years ago? The chapter introduces the work of **archaeologists** and historians.

- **Buildings and walls** — their style, size and material show when and how they were made.
- **Objects found by digging** — coins, pots, tools, jewellery, cannon balls.
- **Writings** — inscriptions on stone, old books, travellers' accounts, and **maps**.

An archaeologist digs very carefully, layer by layer, noting where each thing is found. A broken pot may tell us what people ate and how they cooked; a coin may tell us the king's name and the year.

The textbook also shows an **old map/painting of the fort** and asks you to compare it with today's photo. Some parts have fallen, but the walls still stand — and still tell stories.

Activity: find out about a fort, old temple, mosque, church or monument near you. Who built it? When? What is it made of? Ask an elder for any stories about it.

sections.h: Forts across India and caring for monuments
sections.md:
India has many great forts: **Red Fort** (Delhi), **Chittorgarh** and **Amber** (Rajasthan), **Gwalior**, **Raigad** (Maharashtra, linked with Shivaji), and sea forts like **Janjira**. Many were built on hills, or surrounded by moats, because height and water made attack hard.

Sadly, some visitors scratch names on walls or leave plastic behind. Monuments are our shared heritage; once damaged, they can never be made new again. The **Archaeological Survey of India** protects many of them.

You can help: do not write on walls, do not litter, follow signboards, and tell friends why these walls matter.

parts.md: Ravi clapped under the dome of Fateh Darwaza, and his sister Meena, waiting near the top with Papa, waved her scarf: she had heard it! Ravi grinned. 'No phone, no wires, and it still works after 400 years.'

On the climb, Ravi spotted a bit of clay pipe poking out of a wall. The guide said it once carried water uphill. Ravi imagined bullocks turning a Persian wheel, pots splashing, water travelling all the way to a fountain in the palace garden.
At sunset, from the hilltop, the family saw Hyderabad spread below. Ravi wrote in his diary: 'Walls cannot speak, but if you look carefully, they tell you everything.'

sections.md:
The chapter's fort at Golconda (near Hyderabad) is full of clever clues:
- **Clapping portico:** a clap at the main gate could be heard high up at the top of the fort — an early warning system.
- **Thick walls and huge gates with iron spikes** stopped elephants from ramming them.
- **Water system:** clay pipes and tanks carried water up to the palaces.
- **Cannons and bastions** on the walls show how the fort was defended.
- **Secret tunnels** are said (by local stories) to lead out of the fort; historians are not sure.

Golconda was famous for diamond trade; the Qutb Shahi rulers ruled from here until the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb captured it in 1687.

check.q: Why did fort gates have iron spikes?
check.why: Sharp spikes hurt elephants that were used to push gates open, so they protected the fort.

**Activity:** Visit an old building, temple, mosque, step-well or haveli near you. Look at the walls, carvings and materials. Ask elders what they know, and write: *Who built it? When? What was it used for? What is it used for now?*

rd-school-c5-evs-b.ch11-sunita-in-space.title: Sunita in Space
rd-school-c5-evs-b.ch11-sunita-in-space.subtitle: If the Earth is a ball, why don't people at the bottom fall off? Fly up with Sunita Williams and find out.

sections.md:
**Sunita Williams** is an astronaut of the American space agency **NASA**. Her father came from **Gujarat** in India, so Indian children feel very proud of her. In 2006–07 she lived for about six months on the **International Space Station (ISS)**, a huge laboratory that circles the Earth about 400 km above us, going all the way round roughly every 90 minutes.

The chapter begins with children in a school who are excited by news of Sunita. They have seen her photographs floating in the spaceship, with her hair standing up all around her head! They want to know: *What does the Earth look like from space? Why does she float? How does she eat and sleep?*

Other Indians who went to space: **Rakesh Sharma** (1984, the first Indian in space, in a Soviet mission) and **Kalpana Chawla** (NASA astronaut, flew in 1997 and 2003; she lost her life when the Space Shuttle Columbia broke apart while returning in 2003).

sections.h: The Earth looks like a ball
sections.md:
From space, Sunita said, the Earth looks like a big **round ball**, blue with oceans, white with clouds, brown and green with land. She could not see the borders of countries — only one beautiful planet.

But when we stand on the ground, the Earth looks **flat**. Why? Because the Earth is enormous and we are tiny. Only a very small part of it is near us, and that small part seems flat — just like an ant on a big football would think the ball is flat.

The children in the chapter look at a **globe** — a model of the Earth. They find India, oceans and other continents. A globe is turned on a tilted stand, just like the real Earth spins on its tilted axis.

**Activity: the ship that disappears.** If you watch a ship sailing away on the sea, first its bottom disappears and last its flag at the top — because the Earth's surface curves away. You can try this with a small paper boat moving over a big ball.

check.q: Why does the Earth look flat to us when we stand on it?
options: It is huge and we see only a tiny part
check.why: The Earth is so big that the small part we see around us looks flat, though the whole is round.

sections.md:
The children ask a puzzling question. If the Earth is a ball, then people in countries on the 'bottom' side, like Australia or Chile, should be upside down. Why don't they fall off into space?

The answer is **gravity**. The Earth **pulls everything towards its centre**. So 'down' always means 'towards the middle of the Earth', wherever you stand. A person in India and a person in Brazil both feel their feet pulled to the ground.

That is why:
- A ball thrown up always comes back down.
- Rain falls down, rivers flow downhill.
- Fruit drops from a tree.

**Activity from the chapter:** stick small paper cut-outs of people all around a ball with their feet touching the ball. Turn it. Every person's 'down' points into the ball. Draw arrows from each to the centre.

A different activity: pour water into a bucket, hold the rope and swing it quickly in a full circle over your head (outdoors, carefully!). The water does not fall out while it moves fast. It helps us think about how things can stay going round and round.
keyTerms: Gravity — pull of the Earth towards its centre
Globe — round model of the Earth
Astronaut — person trained to travel in space
Space station — laboratory circling the Earth

check.q: Which way is 'down' for a person anywhere on Earth?
options: Towards the centre of the Earth
check.why: Gravity pulls everything towards the Earth's centre, so down always means towards the middle of the Earth.

sections.md:
In the space station, astronauts **float**. Everything is in free fall around the Earth together, so nothing presses down on the floor. Sunita described:

- **Floating:** You can't just 'sit'; you hook your feet under straps. Pens, spoons and water drops float away if you let go.
- **Hair:** Long hair spreads out in all directions — as in her famous photos.
- **Water:** Water does not pour; it forms floating **balls**. Astronauts drink through a straw from a pouch. There is no normal shower; they wipe with wet towels.
- **Food:** Mostly packed and dried food. Crumbs would float and get into machines, so foods like bread are avoided.
- **Sleeping:** In a sleeping bag tied to a wall so they don't drift.
- **Exercise:** Two hours a day, strapped to a treadmill, because muscles and bones get weak when they don't have to hold the body up.

Sunita even ran a marathon on the treadmill in space in 2007!

check.q: How do astronauts drink water in the space station?
options: From a pouch through a straw
From a tap like at home
check.why: Water floats as blobs in space, so it is kept in closed pouches and sucked through a straw.

sections.h: Where is the sky? Looking at the horizon
sections.md:
The chapter also asks you to observe: where does the sky seem to meet the Earth? That line is called the **horizon**. If you climb higher — onto a roof, a hill or in a plane — you can see further, and the horizon moves away. From space, Sunita could see the horizon as a curved edge, with a thin blue layer of **air** around the Earth.

She also saw that **day and night** happen because the Earth spins: one half faces the Sun (day), the other half is dark (night). From the station she saw about 16 sunrises and 16 sunsets every day!

> **Did you know?** From space at night, cities glow like strings of lights, and you can spot India's coastline by its lit-up towns.

parts.md: Asha, in Class 5 in Ahmedabad, wrote a letter: 'Dear Sunita Didi, my Nani says you are from Gujarat like us. When you float, do you miss sitting on a chair? Do you see our Sabarmati river?'

She imagined the reply: 'Dear Asha, I don't miss chairs, but I miss a hot bath! I can't see small rivers easily, but the whole Earth looks like a glowing blue marble. No lines between countries — just one home for all of us.'
That evening Asha stood on her terrace and watched a bright dot sliding across the sky without blinking. 'Maybe that's the space station,' said Papa. Asha waved, just in case.

The horizon is where the sky seems to meet the land; it moves further as we go higher.

sections.h: Why does the Earth look flat to us?
sections.md:
From space, Sunita Williams saw the Earth as a round ball. But standing in a field it looks flat. Why? The Earth is so huge (about 12,700 km across) that the small part we see at once seems flat — like an ant on a giant football.

**Clue from the sea:** when a ship sails away, first its bottom disappears, then the top of its mast. If the Earth were flat, the whole ship would just get smaller. The line where the sky seems to meet the ground is the **horizon**.

**Activity:** Put a small paper boat on a big ball and move it around the curve while looking from the side — watch it 'sink' bottom-first.

check.q: Which part of a ship sailing away disappears first?
check.why: The curve of the Earth hides the lower part of the ship first, a clue that the Earth is round.

sections.md:
The Earth pulls everything towards itself — this pull is **gravity**. That is why a ball falls down and why 'down' is always towards the Earth's centre, for people in India and in America alike.

In the space station astronauts feel **weightless**: they float, water forms floating drops, and they must:
- strap themselves into sleeping bags tied to walls,
- eat food from packets so crumbs don't float into machines,
- exercise daily on treadmills with straps to keep bones and muscles strong,
- drink through straws from closed pouches.

**Did you know?** Kalpana Chawla, born in Karnal, Haryana, was the first woman of Indian origin in space (1997). Rakesh Sharma was the first Indian in space (1984).

rd-school-c5-evs-b.ch12-what-if-it-finis.title: What if it Finishes...?
rd-school-c5-evs-b.ch12-what-if-it-finis.subtitle: Petrol took millions of years to form and we burn it in minutes. What happens when the tank of the whole world runs dry?

sections.h: A long queue at the petrol pump
sections.md:
The chapter opens with a busy scene. A news report says **petrol prices** are going up from tomorrow. That evening there is a huge **queue** at the petrol pump — scooters, cars, trucks and autos, all honking. A boy, riding with his father, asks: *Why is everyone in such a hurry? What if petrol finishes?*

At the pump, they see signboards showing the price of **petrol** and **diesel** per litre, and a separate line for **CNG** (Compressed Natural Gas). The attendant fills the tank, the meter ticks up — litres on one side, rupees on the other.

This chapter is about **fuels**: what they are, where they come from, why they are running out, and how we can use them wisely.

> **Think:** In your family, what runs on fuel? Count vehicles, stoves, generators and pumps.

A **fuel** is something we burn to get **energy** — heat or movement. Some common fuels:

| Fuel | Used for |
|---|---|
| Petrol | Scooters, cars |
| Diesel | Trucks, buses, trains, tractors, generators, pumps |
| CNG | Autos, buses, taxis in many cities |
| LPG (cooking gas) | Gas stoves in kitchens |
| Kerosene | Lamps and stoves (earlier, widely) |
| Coal | Power stations, factories, old steam engines |
| Wood, cow-dung cakes | Chulhas in villages |

The chapter asks you to make a table of what your family uses fuel for in a day, and whether you could manage without it. Imagine one day with no petrol and no gas: how would you get to school? How would food be cooked?

check.q: Which fuel is commonly used in kitchen gas cylinders?
check.why: LPG, liquefied petroleum gas, is filled in cylinders for cooking on gas stoves.

sections.md:
Petrol, diesel and kerosene all come from **petroleum** (crude oil), a thick dark liquid found deep under the ground and below the sea bed.

How did it form? **Millions of years ago**, tiny plants and animals living in the seas died and sank to the bottom. Layers of sand and mud covered them. Over a very, very long time, heat and pressure deep in the Earth slowly changed them into oil and natural gas. Coal formed in a similar way from ancient forests buried underground. So these are called **fossil fuels**.

People drill wells to pump out crude oil. In India, oil is found in places like **Assam** (Digboi, one of the oldest oil fields in the world), **Gujarat** and offshore at **Mumbai High**. The crude oil goes to a **refinery**, which separates it into petrol, diesel, kerosene, LPG and other products.

The key point: it took **millions of years** to form, but we are using it up in a few hundred years. Once used, it does not come back. That is why it can **finish**.

keyTerms: Fuel — something burnt to get energy
Petroleum — crude oil from under the ground
Fossil fuel — fuel formed from remains of ancient living things
Refinery — factory that separates crude oil into petrol, diesel, etc.

check.q: Why are petrol and diesel called fossil fuels?
options: They are made in factories from water
They formed from remains of ancient living things buried for millions of years
They come from plants grown last year
They come from the Sun directly
check.why: They formed over millions of years from buried remains of tiny sea plants and animals.

sections.md:
Burning petrol and diesel gives out **smoke and harmful gases**. In busy cities, this makes the air dirty and causes coughing, breathing trouble and itchy eyes. Old or badly kept vehicles give more black smoke.

The chapter mentions how **Delhi** changed its buses, autos and taxis to run on **CNG** to reduce pollution. CNG burns more cleanly than diesel, though it is also a fossil fuel.

Vehicles are checked for **PUC (Pollution Under Control)** certificates. Traffic jams waste fuel too: engines keep running while vehicles stand still.

> **Did you know?** The number of vehicles on Indian roads has grown many times in a few decades, so the demand for fuel keeps rising.

sections.h: Prices, and how we can save fuel
sections.md:
Most of India's crude oil is **bought from other countries**, so when world prices rise, our petrol and diesel become costlier, and so do bus fares and even vegetables (they come by truck!).

Ways to save fuel:
1. **Walk or cycle** for short trips.
2. Use **buses, metro and trains** — one bus carries many people.
3. **Car-pool** with neighbours going the same way.
4. **Switch off engines** at red lights and in jams.
5. Keep vehicles serviced and tyres properly filled.
6. In the kitchen: cover pots while cooking, soak dal and rice first, turn off the gas promptly.

And look for energy that does not finish: **solar** (sunlight), **wind**, **water (hydro)** and **biogas** from cow-dung. Solar cookers, solar lamps and electric vehicles charged by solar power are becoming common.

check.q: Which is the best way to save fuel for a 1 km trip to the market?
check.why: Walking or cycling short distances uses no fuel at all and keeps us fit.

parts.md: In Kabir's imagined town, one morning every petrol pump had a sign: 'No petrol'. School buses stood still. Papa's scooter would not start. Vegetable trucks did not arrive.
Kabir dusted off his old cycle. On the way, the roads were silent and the air smelt fresh. Neighbours walked together, chatting. The milkman came on a bicycle cart.

In class, the teacher said, 'One day, this could be real. Let us use fuel like a treasure.' Kabir's group drew a plan: solar panels on the school roof, a cycle stand, and a 'Switch off at the signal' campaign.

summary: A fuel is burnt to give energy for heat or movement.
Petrol, diesel, CNG, LPG, kerosene, coal and wood are common fuels.

Petroleum and coal formed over millions of years from remains of living things — fossil fuels.
Crude oil is separated in refineries; India has oil in Assam, Gujarat and Mumbai High.
Fossil fuels will finish because we use them far faster than they form.
Burning fuels causes smoke and air pollution; Delhi shifted public transport to CNG.
India imports much of its oil, so prices affect everything we buy.
Save fuel: walk, cycle, use public transport, car-pool, switch off engines.
Solar, wind, water and biogas are energy sources that do not run out.

rd-school-c5-evs-b.ch12-what-if-it-finis.title: What if it Finishes...? (part 2)
rd-school-c5-evs-b.ch12-what-if-it-finis.subtitle: How petrol forms, what pollution costs us, and a fuel-saving action plan

sections.md:
Petrol, diesel and kerosene are made from **crude oil (petroleum)** found deep under the ground and the sea bed. It formed over **millions of years** from tiny plants and animals buried under layers of mud and rock, pressed and heated. We pump it out through wells, and refineries separate it into petrol, diesel, kerosene, LPG and more.

Because it takes millions of years to form and we use it in a few years, it is a **non-renewable** resource. Coal and natural gas are similar. Sun, wind and flowing water are **renewable** — they do not run out.

left.title: Non-renewable
points: Takes millions of years to form

check.q: Why is petrol called non-renewable?
options: It takes millions of years to form
check.why: Nature needs millions of years to make petroleum, so once used it cannot be replaced in our lifetime.

sections.md:
Burning petrol and diesel gives out smoke and gases. In busy cities like Delhi, people suffer coughing, burning eyes and asthma, especially in winter. Smoke also warms the Earth. And fuel prices rise when supply is short, so travel and food become costlier.

**Activity from the chapter:** Make a survey of your family. How many vehicles do you have? What fuel do they use? How much is spent each month? What else uses fuel at home — the LPG stove, generator, pump?

**Did you know?** CNG buses in Delhi, started in the early 2000s, helped reduce some air pollution compared with diesel buses.

check.q: Which is a renewable energy source?
check.why: Wind keeps blowing naturally and will not run out, so it is renewable.

sections.md:
- Walk or cycle short distances.
- Share rides; use buses and the metro.
- Switch off the engine at red lights.
- Keep tyres properly filled and vehicles serviced.
- Cover the pot while cooking and soak dal first — less LPG.
- Use solar cookers and solar water heaters where possible.
- Switch off lights and fans when not needed (much electricity comes from coal).

Make a poster: *Save fuel today, so it's there tomorrow.*

summary: Petroleum formed underground over millions of years.

rd-school-c5-evs-b.ch7-experiments-with-.title: Experiments with Water
rd-school-c5-evs-b.ch7-experiments-with-.subtitle: Why does an egg sink in tap water but float in salty water? Grab a glass and become a scientist.

sections.md:
The chapter opens with a news-style story. A man who could not swim fell into a sea, and yet he **did not drown** — he kept floating! This happened in the **Dead Sea**, a lake between Israel and Jordan whose water is so **salty** that people float on it easily, even lying back and reading a newspaper.

Why does salty water hold us up better? To find out, the chapter asks us to do experiments — just like real scientists: **guess** (predict), **try**, **observe** and **conclude**.

> **Scientist's rule:** write your guess *before* the experiment, then write what really happened. It is fine if the guess was wrong — that is how we learn!

Take a bucket of water and collect things: a coin, a pencil, a leaf, a plastic bottle cap, a stone, a piece of wood, a steel spoon, a key, a paper ball, a rubber band, a candle.

First **guess** for each: will it float or sink? Write it in a table. Then drop them in one by one.

| Object | My guess | What happened |
|---|---|---|
| Coin | ? | sinks |
| Wood | ? | floats |
| Stone | ? | sinks |
| Leaf | ? | floats |
| Plastic cap | ? | floats |

You'll find that it is not only about how **heavy** something is. A big log floats but a tiny pin sinks! **Shape** matters too: a lump of clay sinks, but if you shape the same clay into a little bowl, it can float. That is why huge iron ships float — their shape is hollow and spread out.

**Try more:** Does a paper ball float for ever, or does it sink after soaking? What happens to an empty bottle, and to the same bottle filled with water?

check.q: Why can a large iron ship float?
options: Its hollow, spread-out shape lets it float
check.why: A ship's hollow, wide shape pushes aside a lot of water, which holds it up even though iron alone would sink.

sections.md:
Here is the famous experiment.

1. Fill a glass with plain tap water. Gently put in a raw egg. It **sinks** to the bottom.
2. Take the egg out. Add salt, one spoon at a time, stirring well.
3. Put the egg back after each spoon. After several spoons, the egg starts to **rise** and then **floats**!

What happened? Dissolving salt makes the water **heavier for the same amount** (denser). Denser water pushes up more strongly, so it can hold up the egg. That is exactly why the very salty Dead Sea holds up people, and why it is a little easier to float in the sea than in a river or swimming pool.

**Extra challenge:** fill half a glass with salty water, then slowly pour plain water on top along a spoon. Put the egg in — it may stop and float right in the middle!

fig.alt: Two glasses: egg at bottom of plain water; in the other, salt falls in and the egg rises.

check.q: What makes the egg float in the second glass?
options: Adding salt makes the water denser
check.why: Dissolved salt makes water denser, so it pushes up the egg strongly enough to float it.

sections.md:
Now take several glasses of water. Into each put one spoon of: **sugar, salt, sand, chalk powder, oil, sawdust, washing powder, turmeric**. Stir and wait a few minutes.

- **Sugar** and **salt** seem to **disappear** — they **dissolve**. You cannot see them, but taste tells you they are there (only taste in a clean glass with an adult's permission!).
- **Sand** and **chalk** settle at the bottom — they do **not dissolve**.
- **Oil** floats as a layer on top — it does not mix.
- **Sawdust** floats.

Does sugar dissolve faster in hot water or cold water? Try it — warm water wins. Does stirring help? Yes! What if you keep adding sugar? After a point, no more dissolves; it stays at the bottom.

**Getting things back:** Pour salty water into a plate and keep it in the sun. The water slowly goes into the air — **evaporation** — leaving salt behind. This is how **salt is made from sea water** in salt pans along the coasts of Gujarat and Tamil Nadu.
keyTerms: Float — stay on the surface of water
Sink — go down to the bottom
Dissolve — mix completely so it can't be seen
Evaporation — water changing into vapour and going into the air

check.q: Which of these will NOT dissolve in water?
check.why: Sand does not dissolve; it settles at the bottom while sugar and salt mix completely.

sections.h: Salt and freedom: the Dandi March
sections.md:
Salt from the sea connects to a great moment in India's freedom struggle. Under British rule there was a **tax on salt**, and Indians were not allowed to make their own salt freely — even though it is something every poor family needs.

In **1930**, **Mahatma Gandhi** set out from **Sabarmati Ashram** in Ahmedabad and walked about 385 km with his followers to the seaside village of **Dandi** in Gujarat. The walk took 24 days. At Dandi he picked up a handful of natural salt, breaking the unjust law. Across India, thousands followed by making salt. This **Salt Satyagraha** (Dandi March) showed the world the power of peaceful protest.

> **Did you know?** Some salt we eat has **iodine** added (iodised salt), which keeps our body healthy.

sections.h: Water in the air: where do the drops come from?
sections.md:
The chapter ends with a puzzle. Put ice in a steel glass and wait. Soon tiny **drops of water** appear on the **outside** of the glass! They did not leak through. They came from the **air** — the air always has invisible water vapour, which turns back into drops when it touches the cold glass (**condensation**). It is the same reason grass is wet with **dew** on winter mornings.

So water keeps changing: liquid → vapour (evaporation) → liquid again (condensation). This is part of the **water cycle** that brings us rain.

parts.md: Meenu borrowed an egg from Amma's basket and a big glass. 'It'll sink,' said her brother. It did. Then Meenu tipped in salt, spoon after spoon. On the sixth spoon, the egg wobbled up and bobbed. Her brother's mouth fell open.
Next, she left a plate of salty water on the terrace. By evening, a crust of white crystals sparkled on the plate. 'You made salt!' laughed Amma. 'Just like the salt pans near Tuticorin.'
In her notebook Meenu wrote: Guess, Try, See, Think. Her teacher pinned the page on the class board under the title 'Our Scientist of the Week'.

summary: In the very salty Dead Sea, people float easily.
Scientists predict, test, observe and then conclude.
Whether things float depends on weight and shape — a hollow ship floats.
An egg sinks in plain water but floats when enough salt is dissolved.
Salt water is denser and pushes up objects more strongly.
Sugar and salt dissolve; sand and chalk do not; oil floats on top.
Warm water and stirring make things dissolve faster; there is a limit to how much dissolves.
Evaporation leaves salt behind — salt is made this way from sea water.
Gandhiji's Dandi March in 1930 broke the unfair salt law.
Drops on a cold glass come from water vapour in the air (condensation).

How can the same clay be made to sink and to float?
Describe the floating egg experiment step by step.

rd-school-c5-evs-b.ch7-experiments-with-.title: Experiments with Water (part 2)
rd-school-c5-evs-b.ch7-experiments-with-.subtitle: Sink or float, dissolving, the Dandi salt story, and an egg that floats

sections.md:
Drop different things into a bucket of water and note what happens. Make a table and guess first, then test.

Things that float are usually light for their size (wood, plastic bottle cap, leaf, cork). Things that sink are heavy for their size (stone, coin, key). Shape matters too: a flat sheet of foil floats but the same foil crushed into a tight ball may sink.

check.why: Cork is very light for its size, so water holds it up.

sections.md:
Stir salt or sugar into water — it seems to vanish, but taste tells you it is still there. It has **dissolved**. Sand, chalk powder and oil do **not** dissolve.

Warm water dissolves sugar faster than cold water, and stirring helps.

How to get the salt back? Leave the salty water in a plate in the sun. The water **evaporates** and white salt is left. This is how salt is made from sea water in pans in Gujarat and Tamil Nadu.

**Did you know?** In 1930 Mahatma Gandhi walked about 385 km from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi to make salt from sea water, breaking the British salt law — the **Dandi March**.

check.q: How do we get salt back from salty water?
check.why: When the water evaporates in the sun, the dissolved salt is left behind.

sections.md:
Put an egg in a glass of plain water — it sinks. Now add salt spoon by spoon and stir. After several spoons the egg rises and floats! Salty water is heavier (denser) and pushes up more strongly. That is why it is easier to float in the sea than in a river, and very easy in the extremely salty Dead Sea.

**Also in the chapter:** a lump of jaggery or a drop of ink spreads in water; oil floats as a layer on top of water and does not mix.

rd-school-c5-evs-b.ch8-a-treat-for-mosqu.title: A Treat for Mosquitoes
rd-school-c5-evs-b.ch8-a-treat-for-mosqu.subtitle: A fever that comes with shivering, a blood test and a tiny insect — how do we fight malaria?

sections.md:
The chapter begins with a girl who has had a **high fever** for several days. The fever comes with **shivering and chills**, then she sweats and feels very weak. Her family remembers that many children in the neighbourhood have the same problem.

The doctor asks about the fever and then advises a **blood test**. A tiny drop of blood is taken from her finger, placed on a glass slide and looked at under a **microscope**. The report says she has **malaria**. She is given medicine and gets better after completing the full course.

The chapter asks: *What causes malaria? How does it spread from person to person? And why does it rise after the rains?*

> **Important:** if anyone has a fever, see a doctor. Do not guess or take medicines on your own.

Malaria is caused by a **tiny germ** (a parasite) that lives in the blood. It is far too small to see without a microscope.

It is spread by the **female Anopheles mosquito**:
1. The mosquito bites a person who already has malaria and sucks blood with the germs.
2. The germs grow inside the mosquito for some days.
3. When this mosquito bites a healthy person, the germs enter that person's blood.
4. After some days, the new person gets fever with shivering.

Only the **female** mosquito bites people; she needs blood to lay eggs. Males drink plant juices. *Anopheles* mosquitoes mostly bite at **dusk and night**.

**Did you know?** In **1897**, **Ronald Ross**, a British doctor working in India, showed in **Secunderabad** (near Hyderabad) that mosquitoes carry malaria. He received the Nobel Prize in 1902.

fig.alt: Mosquito flying from an ill person to a healthy person along a curved path.

check.q: Which mosquito spreads malaria?
check.why: Only the female Anopheles mosquito bites people and carries malaria germs from one person to another.

sections.md:
Mosquitoes lay their **eggs in still water**. A mosquito's life has four stages:

**egg → larva → pupa → adult mosquito**

The eggs float on water. The **larvae** (wrigglers) hang just under the surface, breathing air through a tube. In about a week to ten days, adults fly away.

Any **standing water** can become a nursery: puddles, blocked drains, ponds, old tyres, broken pots, coconut shells, flower vases, coolers, overhead tanks without lids, even water in a bottle cap! This is why mosquitoes and malaria **increase after the monsoon**.

**Activity from the chapter:** do a survey around your school or home. Where do you see water collected? Mark the places on a simple map. Who should clean each place — your family, the school, or the municipality?

head: Stage
Where
Looks like
rows: On the surface of still water
fig.caption: Life cycle of a mosquito.

keyTerms: Malaria — disease with fever and shivering spread by Anopheles mosquito
Larva — young wriggling stage living in water
Microscope — instrument to see very tiny things
Breeding — producing young ones

check.q: Why do mosquitoes increase after the rains?
options: Rain leaves pools of still water where they lay eggs
check.why: Rainwater collects in puddles and containers, and mosquitoes breed in this still water.

sections.md:
Mosquitoes spread other diseases too.

- **Dengue** and **chikungunya** are spread by the **Aedes** mosquito, which has **black and white stripes** on its body and legs. It bites mostly during the **day** and breeds in **clean** stored water — coolers, flower pots, tyres, water drums.
- Dengue causes high fever, body and joint pain, and sometimes a fall in platelets, which can be serious. Chikungunya causes very painful joints.

Newspapers report these diseases, especially in cities, after the rains. Some cities spray medicine or release small fish (like **Gambusia**) into ponds that eat mosquito larvae.

We can stop mosquitoes **breeding** and stop them **biting**.

**Stop breeding:**
1. Do not let water stand. Empty coolers, pots and tyres at least once a week.
2. Cover water tanks and containers.
3. Fill up pits and puddles; keep drains flowing.
4. Put a few drops of kerosene or oil on still water that cannot be drained, so larvae can't breathe (done by adults or health workers).

**Stop biting:**
1. Sleep under a **mosquito net**.
2. Wear long sleeves in the evening.
3. Use screens on windows; use mosquito repellents carefully.

If someone has fever, they should get a blood test and take the **full course** of medicines the doctor gives.

check.q: Which is the best way to stop mosquitoes breeding near home?
options: Keep old tyres full of water
Empty and cover containers of water every week
check.why: Mosquitoes breed in still water, so emptying and covering containers removes their nurseries.

sections.h: Blood, anaemia and a healthy diet
sections.md:
The chapter also talks about **blood**. In the microscope, the doctor also checks the **red blood cells**. Some children's blood shows they have **anaemia** — not enough healthy red blood. Signs are tiredness, pale skin, nails and tongue, and getting breathless easily.

Anaemia is often due to lack of **iron** in food. Foods rich in iron include **green leafy vegetables** (spinach, methi, amaranth), **jaggery (gur)**, **amla**, dates, pulses, beans and sprouts. Vitamin C (lemon, amla, guava) helps the body absorb iron. Many schools give iron tablets under health programmes, as advised by doctors.

> **Think:** Does your school mid-day meal or your lunch box have something green every day?

parts.md: When Ruchi got malaria, her classmates in Nagpur were worried. After she got better, she told them how the doctor saw the germs through a microscope. 'And they came from a mosquito near our water tank,' she said.
The class formed 'Mosquito Detectives'. With torches and notebooks, they found larvae in a broken pot, a cooler and an old tyre behind the canteen. They drew a map with red crosses.
Every Sunday became 'Dry Day' in their colony: empty, scrub, cover. By Diwali, the Detectives proudly reported: not a single fever case on their street this season.

summary: Malaria causes fever with shivering; a blood test under a microscope confirms it.
Malaria germs are spread by the female Anopheles mosquito, which bites mostly at night.
Ronald Ross proved in 1897, in Secunderabad, that mosquitoes spread malaria.
Mosquitoes lay eggs in still water; stages are egg, larva, pupa, adult.
Mosquitoes increase after the rains because of collected water.
Aedes mosquitoes (striped, day-biting) spread dengue and chikungunya.
Stop breeding: empty, cover and drain water; fish like Gambusia eat larvae.
Stop bites: nets, long sleeves, window screens.
Always see a doctor for fever and complete the full medicine course.
Anaemia means too little healthy blood; iron-rich food like greens, jaggery and amla helps.

Explain with a diagram how malaria spreads from one person to another.
Draw the life cycle of a mosquito.
List five places near your home where mosquitoes may breed.
How is the Aedes mosquito different from Anopheles?

rd-school-c5-evs-b.ch8-a-treat-for-mosqu.title: A Treat for Mosquitoes (part 2)
rd-school-c5-evs-b.ch8-a-treat-for-mosqu.subtitle: The mosquito life cycle, blood tests, Ronald Ross and a mosquito survey

sections.md:
A mosquito lays eggs on **still water** — in coolers, tyres, pots, tanks and puddles. In a few days:
1. **Egg** hatches into
2. **Larva** (wriggler) living in water, then
3. **Pupa**, then
4. **Adult mosquito** that flies away.

The whole cycle can take about a week to ten days. So emptying stagnant water **once a week** breaks the cycle. Only female mosquitoes bite and drink blood; males feed on plant juices.

check.q: Why should coolers be emptied every week?

check.why: Mosquitoes take about a week to grow from egg to adult, so weekly emptying kills larvae first.

sections.h: Testing blood and a great discovery
sections.md:
In the story, a doctor sends a sick child for a **blood test**. A drop of blood is seen under a **microscope**; if the malaria germ (a tiny parasite) is found, the doctor gives the right medicine. Other diseases from mosquitoes include **dengue and chikungunya** (spread by the striped Aedes mosquito that bites by day).

**Did you know?** In 1897, Ronald Ross, working in Secunderabad, showed that malaria germs are carried by mosquitoes. He received the Nobel Prize in 1902.

check.q: Which tool helps see malaria germs in blood?
check.why: Germs are too small for our eyes, so a microscope magnifies the blood drop.

sections.md:
Walk around your school or colony with a teacher. Note places where water collects: broken pots, tyres, flower vases, roof tanks without lids, blocked drains. Make a table of place, problem and solution. Share it with the school or RWA. Cover tanks, drain puddles, add kerosene or larva-eating **gambusia fish** to ponds, use nets and repellents, and wear full sleeves.

Anaemia is also mentioned in the chapter: lack of iron makes people tired and pale; eating green leafy vegetables, jaggery and amla helps (see a doctor for treatment).

summary: Mosquitoes breed in still water.
Life cycle: egg, larva, pupa, adult — about a week.
Only females bite.
Malaria is found by a blood test under a microscope.
Dengue and chikungunya are spread by Aedes mosquitoes.
Ronald Ross linked malaria to mosquitoes in 1897.
Empty water weekly, cover tanks, use nets.
Iron-rich food helps prevent anaemia.
