rd-school-c5-evs-b.ch9-up-you-go.title: Up You Go!
rd-school-c5-evs-b.ch9-up-you-go.subtitle: Ropes, rocks, icy rivers and the roof of the world — join a mountaineering camp and climb with courage.

sections.md:
The chapter is written like the diary of a girl who goes to a **mountaineering camp** in the Himalayas with other children, under trained instructors. They travel by bus up winding roads, see snowy peaks for the first time, and camp in tents near a river.

The first rule the instructors give: **safety and teamwork**. Nobody climbs alone. Everyone listens, helps and checks each other's equipment. The children also learn to **respect the mountains** — not to litter, not to shout near snow slopes, and to carry back all waste.

In India, mountaineering is taught at institutes such as the **Nehru Institute of Mountaineering** in Uttarkashi (Uttarakhand) and the **Himalayan Mountaineering Institute** in Darjeeling (West Bengal).

sections.h: Rock climbing and the trusty rope
sections.md:
On day one, the children learn **rock climbing**. They face a steep rock wall.

- They wear a **harness** around the waist and legs, attached to a strong **rope**.
- The rope passes through metal clips called **karabiners** fixed to the rock.
- A partner below, the **belayer**, holds the rope tight. If the climber slips, the rope catches them.
- Climbers look for **holds** — cracks and bumps for fingers and toes — and keep **three points of contact** (two hands and one foot, or two feet and one hand) on the rock.

Coming down is done by **rappelling**: leaning back, walking down the rock while the rope slides slowly through a device.

The diary-writer is scared at first, but her friends cheer her on. When she reaches the top, she feels she can do anything! The lesson: **trust** your team and your training.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 340' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='340' fill='#e1f5fe'/><path d='M200 340 L260 40 L420 40 L480 340Z' fill='#8d6e63'/><circle cx='330' cy='45' r='6' fill='#ffc107'/><line x1='330' y1='45' x2='150' y2='320' stroke='#e91e63' stroke-width='3'/><g><circle r='10' fill='#ff7043'/><rect x='-6' y='10' width='12' height='22' fill='#3949ab'/><animateMotion dur='6s' repeatCount='indefinite' path='M330 300 L330 70 L330 300'/></g><circle cx='150' cy='300' r='10' fill='#43a047'/><rect x='144' y='310' width='12' height='22' fill='#2e7d32'/><g font-size='14' fill='#263238'><text x='345' y='50'>karabiner</text><text x='40' y='300'>belayer</text><text x='440' y='180'>climber</text></g></svg>
fig.caption: The rope runs from the climber through a karabiner at the top to the belayer, who keeps it tight.
fig.alt: Climber going up a rock face on a rope held by a partner on the ground.

keyTerms: Harness — belt with leg loops tied to the rope
Karabiner — metal clip with a spring gate
Belayer — partner who holds the climber's rope
Rappelling — coming down a rock using a rope

check.q: What does a belayer do?
options: Holds the climber's rope tight to catch a fall
check.why: The belayer controls the rope from below so a slipping climber is caught safely.

sections.md:
Next, the group must cross a fast, icy **mountain stream**. The instructors fix a rope across it. The children:
- cross one at a time, holding the rope,
- walk sideways, facing upstream,
- test each step before putting weight on a stone.

Sometimes a **'Tyrolean traverse'** is used — a rope tied tight over the river, and you slide across hanging from it in a harness!

The girl's shoes get soaked, her feet go numb with cold, and yet everyone laughs at the end. In the evening they dry clothes by the fire and share **food** — hot dal, rice, khichdi, and lots of tea. At height, **water** and food matter a lot: the body burns energy to stay warm.

check.q: While crossing a mountain stream, what should you do?
options: Hold the fixed rope and test each step
Cross in a big group holding hands without a rope
check.why: Holding a fixed rope and testing each foothold keeps you steady against the strong current.

sections.h: Packing a rucksack and living in tents
sections.md:
The children learn to pack a **rucksack** for a trek:

| Must carry | Why |
|---|---|
| Warm clothes, cap, gloves | It gets very cold at height |
| Raincoat | Weather changes fast |
| Water bottle | Avoid dehydration |
| Torch | Nights are dark |
| First-aid kit | Cuts, sprains |
| Dry food (chana, gur, dry fruits) | Quick energy |
| Sunglasses and sunscreen | Snow reflects strong sunlight |

Heavy things go **close to the back**, light things on top. They also pitch **tents**, tie guy ropes, and keep shoes inside so they don't freeze.

High up, the **air is thin** (less oxygen), so people feel breathless and must climb slowly, resting often. Climbers spend days getting used to the height (**acclimatisation**).

check.q: Why must climbers move slowly at great heights?
check.why: Air at great heights is thin with less oxygen, so the body gets tired quickly and needs time to adjust.

sections.md:
**Mount Everest** (about 8,849 m) on the border of **Nepal and China (Tibet)** is the highest mountain in the world. People in Nepal call it **Sagarmatha**; in Tibet it is **Chomolungma**.

- On **29 May 1953**, **Tenzing Norgay** (a Sherpa mountaineer) and **Edmund Hillary** (from New Zealand) became the first people known to reach its top.
- In **1984**, **Bachendri Pal** became the **first Indian woman** to climb Everest. She later trained many young climbers.
- Since then, many Indians have climbed it, including teenagers, and people from the Army and police.

The chapter also shows the **Indian flag** being placed on a summit and asks how climbers might feel at that moment.

The **Sherpas** of Nepal and Sikkim/Darjeeling are famous for their skill and strength in the high mountains.

items.what: Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary first reach Everest's summit
First successful Indian expedition to Everest
Bachendri Pal — first Indian woman on Everest
Mountaineering institutes train young Indians every year

fig.caption: Milestones on the roof of the world.

sections.md:
At the end of camp, the children write what they learned:
- **Courage** is not 'no fear'; it is doing something even when you are scared, safely.
- **Teamwork**: on a rope, everyone's safety depends on each other.
- **Patience**: the mountain is climbed one step at a time.
- **Respect for nature**: carry back your waste; mountains are home to people, animals and rivers that feed the plains.

> **Think:** Have you ever done something you were scared of? Who helped you? Write about it.

parts.md: Neha stared at the rock. Her legs shook. 'I can't.' Below, her partner Tashi held the rope firm. 'I've got you. Find the next hold.' Neha reached, found a crack, and pulled herself up.
Halfway, she froze. Tashi called, 'Three points on the rock! Breathe!' She breathed, moved a foot, then a hand. The top came closer, until she touched the big karabiner and shouted with joy.
That night, around the fire, Neha said, 'The rope didn't climb for me, but it made me brave.' Tashi smiled. 'Tomorrow, you hold the rope for me.'

rd-school-c5-evs-b.ch9-up-you-go-2.title: Up You Go! (part 2)
rd-school-c5-evs-b.ch9-up-you-go-2.subtitle: Bachendri Pal, teamwork, mountain safety and the chapter's activities

sections.h: Bachendri Pal: the first Indian woman on Everest
sections.md:
The chapter's camp is run by **Bachendri Pal**, who in **May 1984** became the **first Indian woman to climb Mount Everest** (8,848 m). She grew up in a village in the hills of Uttarakhand, where walking up steep slopes to school was everyday life. Many people told her that climbing was not a job for a girl, but she trained hard and joined an Indian expedition.

Near the top, the air is so thin that climbers carry **oxygen cylinders**. Winds are freezing and a storm can come suddenly. In her team's camp, an avalanche buried tents at night; she survived and still went on to the summit. At the top she planted the Indian flag.

**Did you know?** The first people known to reach Everest's summit were **Tenzing Norgay** and **Edmund Hillary**, on 29 May 1953.

check.q: Why do climbers carry oxygen cylinders near Everest's top?
options: Because the air there has very little oxygen
check.why: High up the air is thin, so each breath gives far less oxygen and climbers need extra from cylinders.

sections.md:
At camp the children learn that in the mountains **nobody climbs alone**. Ropes link a team; one person anchors while another moves. Rules the chapter stresses:

- Listen to the instructor and follow signals.
- Check knots, harness and shoes before every climb.
- Never throw stones or litter — carry all waste back down.
- Drink water, wear layers, and protect skin and eyes from strong sun and snow glare.
- Help the slowest member; the team is only as strong as its last climber.

**Activities to try:** Make a list of things you would pack for a three-day camp and give a reason for each. Talk to someone who has gone trekking. Find on a map of India the states with high mountains (Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Sikkim, Arunachal Pradesh). Think: Have you ever done something brave that others thought you couldn't do? Write about how it felt.
keyTerms: expedition — an organised journey with a goal
summit — the very top of a mountain
avalanche — a sudden fall of snow down a slope

check.q: Which is the best mountain rule?
check.why: Mountains are fragile and hard to clean, so climbers carry every bit of rubbish back with them.

Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary first reached the summit in 1953.
Air is thin at great heights; climbers use oxygen.
Ropes and teamwork keep climbers safe.

Courage means trying even when others doubt you.

rd-school-c5-evs-c.ch13-a-shelter-so-hig.title: A Shelter so High!
rd-school-c5-evs-c.ch13-a-shelter-so-hig.subtitle: Tents of yak hair at 4,500 metres, mud houses with flat roofs, homes that float on a lake — how people build for cold heights.

sections.h: Life on the high plateau of Changthang
sections.md:
Far up in **Ladakh**, in the east, lies a cold, windy, high land called **Changthang**, about 4,500 metres above sea level. It is so cold that winter temperatures fall far below zero, and there is very little rain or snow. Grass is short and scattered.

Here live the **Changpa** people. They are **nomads (pastoralists)**: they keep herds of **yaks, sheep and goats** and move from place to place in search of grass for their animals, carrying their homes with them.

The chapter is told by a Changpa boy, who describes his family's life: moving camp several times a year, looking after animals, and living in a special tent called a **rebo**.

> **Think:** If you had to carry your whole house with you, what would you make it from?

sections.h: The rebo: a tent that fights the cold
sections.md:
A **rebo** is a tent made from **yak hair**. It is clever in many ways:

- **Yak wool is woven into strips** by the family and stitched together. It is strong and keeps out wind and cold.
- The tent is held up with **poles** and ropes, and its edges are pinned down with stones.
- A pit is dug about 2 feet deep, and the tent is put up over it; a low **wall of mud bricks or stones** around it stops icy wind.
- An opening at the top lets **smoke out** from the stove, which burns dried dung and twigs.
- Inside, the family sleeps on rugs; spaces for cooking, sleeping and a small prayer corner.

It takes only a short time to fold the rebo and load it onto yaks and horses when the family moves. A rebo can last for many years if repaired.

fig.alt: Dark tent on a high cold plain with a low wall around it and smoke rising from the top.

keyTerms: Nomad — person who moves from place to place with animals
Rebo — Changpa tent woven from yak hair
Pashmina — very fine wool from the Changthang goat
Plateau — high, flat land

check.q: What is a rebo made of?
check.why: The Changpa weave yak hair into strips and stitch them into a warm, windproof tent called a rebo.

sections.md:
For the Changpa, animals are everything: food, milk, wool, transport and income.

- **Yaks** give milk, meat, hair for tents and ropes, and carry loads.
- **Sheep** give wool.
- The **Changthangi goat** grows a very soft, warm under-coat to survive the cold. This is **pashmina**, one of the finest wools in the world. In early summer the goats' fleece is **combed**, not cut, to collect it.

Pashmina is sent to **Kashmir**, where skilled weavers make the famous **pashmina shawls**. A real pashmina shawl is so fine and soft it can be very expensive.

The family moves camps through the year — the **children** help too — and the elders know exactly which pastures to use in which season so grass is not finished.

check.q: Where does pashmina wool come from?
check.why: Pashmina is the soft under-coat combed from Changthangi goats that survive the cold of Changthang.

sections.md:
In Ladakh villages that do not move, houses are built to keep heat in:

- Walls are thick, made of **stone and sun-dried mud bricks**, often plastered with mud and painted white.
- **Flat roofs** of wooden beams, twigs and mud, because there is very little rain. The roof is used to dry vegetables, apricots and fodder and to store wood for winter.
- Houses are often **two or three storeys**. In winter, the family lives on the **ground floor**, which stays warmer; animals are kept in a part of the lower floor too and their warmth helps. In summer, people use the upper floor.
- **Windows** are small, so less cold air enters, and a central kitchen stove (with a chimney) warms the house.

Ladakhi **gompas** (monasteries) stand high on hills, white and beautiful.

check.q: Why do Ladakhi houses have flat roofs?
options: There is very little rain, and the roof is used for drying and storage
check.why: Ladakh is very dry, so a flat mud roof works and is useful for drying crops and storing fuel.

sections.md:
The chapter then moves to the **Kashmir valley**, where it is cold in winter but there are more rains and snow.

- Some old houses have **sloping roofs** so snow slides off.
- **Dhajji** houses use a wooden frame filled with small bricks or stones and mud. Wood bends a little, so such houses are safer in **earthquakes**.
- **Houseboats** float on the **Dal Lake** and Jhelum river in Srinagar. They are made of wood, with carved ceilings, and have rooms for families and tourists. **Shikaras** (small boats) carry people across the lake; there are even floating vegetable markets.
- In winter, Kashmiris keep warm with a **kangri** — a small clay pot of hot coals in a wicker basket, held under a long woollen gown called a **pheran**.

The nomadic **Gujjar and Bakarwal** shepherds also move with their animals between the hills and plains, living in simple houses or tents.

right.title: Kashmir valley
points: Cold winters, more snow and rain

check.q: What is a kangri?
options: A clay pot of hot coals in a basket used for warmth
check.why: A kangri is a wicker-covered clay pot with hot coals that Kashmiris hold under their pheran in winter.

parts.md: At dawn, Tsering's mother folded the rebo while he and his sister rounded up the goats. Their breath made clouds in the cold air. 'The grass near the lake is ready,' said Grandfather.
The yaks were loaded: tent strips, poles, pots, rugs. By noon, they reached the new camp. Everyone dug the shallow pit, raised the poles and stretched the tent. The stove was lit before sunset.
That summer, a trader came for the pashmina. Months later, a postcard arrived from Srinagar with a photo of a shawl. 'From our goats,' Tsering smiled, 'to the world.'

summary: Changthang in Ladakh is a high, cold, dry plateau about 4,500 m high.
The Changpa are nomads who herd yaks, sheep and goats and move for grass.
They live in rebos — tents woven from yak hair, set over a pit with a low wall.
Smoke from the stove escapes through an opening at the top.
Changthangi goats give pashmina, combed and woven into shawls in Kashmir.
Ladakhi village houses have thick mud-stone walls, small windows and flat roofs.
In winter Ladakhi families live on the warmer ground floor.
Kashmir houses may have sloping roofs and earthquake-safe dhajji walls.
Houseboats and shikaras float on Dal Lake in Srinagar.
A kangri under the pheran keeps Kashmiris warm in winter.

rd-school-c5-evs-c.ch13-a-shelter-so-hig.title: A Shelter so High! (part 2)
rd-school-c5-evs-c.ch13-a-shelter-so-hig.subtitle: Houseboats, homes across India and why houses differ

sections.md:
In Srinagar, many families live on **houseboats** on the Dal and Jhelum waters. A houseboat is made of wood, often deodar or cedar, and can be long, with a sitting room, bedrooms and a kitchen. Small boats called **shikaras** carry people, vegetables and flowers between houseboats and the shore. There is even a floating vegetable market early in the morning.

Kashmiri homes on land often have sloping roofs so snow slides off, thick walls of stone or brick, and wooden ceilings with carved patterns (**khatamband**). In cold months people keep warm with a **kangri** — a small clay pot of hot coals in a woven wicker basket, held under the long woollen cloak called the **pheran**.

check.q: What is a kangri?
options: A clay pot of coals in a wicker basket used for warmth
check.why: The kangri holds burning coals and is kept under the pheran to warm the body in winter.

sections.md:
The chapter ends by asking why houses look so different across India. The answer: people build with **what is nearby** and for **the weather they face**.

| Place | Home | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Changthang | rebo tent of yak hair | moves with herds, keeps out wind |
| Ladakh | stone-and-mud house, flat roof | little rain; roof dries crops |
| Kashmir | sloping roof, houseboat | snow; lakes |
| Assam, flood areas | houses on bamboo stilts | water rises in rain |
| Rajasthan | thick mud walls, small windows | heat and sand |
| Kerala | sloping tiled roofs | heavy rain |

**Activities:** Draw your own house and label what it is made of. Ask elders how homes in your area have changed. Compare: which homes can move and which cannot?

check.q: Why are houses in Assam often raised on stilts?
check.why: Stilts lift the floor above rising water during heavy rain and floods.

summary: Houseboats float on the Dal Lake; shikaras link them to shore.
Kashmiri houses have sloping roofs for snow and carved wooden ceilings.
Kangri and pheran keep people warm.
Homes are built from local materials to suit local weather.
Stilt houses suit floods; mud houses suit heat; flat roofs suit dry Ladakh.

rd-school-c5-evs-c.ch14-when-the-earth-s.title: When the Earth Shook!
rd-school-c5-evs-c.ch14-when-the-earth-s.subtitle: One Republic Day morning in Kutch the ground began to roll. What happened next — and how do we stay safe?

sections.md:
The chapter begins with a girl from a village in **Kutch**, Gujarat, telling her story. It was **26 January 2001**, Republic Day. Children were getting ready for school celebrations when, at about 8:46 in the morning, the ground began to **shake violently**. Utensils fell, walls cracked, and in less than a minute many houses collapsed.

This was the **Gujarat (Bhuj) earthquake**. Thousands of people lost their lives and many more were injured; lakhs of homes were damaged, especially in Bhuj, Anjar, Bhachau and nearby villages. The girl's family survived, but their house was broken, and some neighbours were lost.

The chapter is calm and gentle: it asks how people felt, how they helped each other, and what we can learn to be safer.

> **Talk:** Have you or your elders ever felt an earthquake, flood or cyclone? What did you do?

The Earth's outer layer is made of huge pieces of rock called **plates**, which move very, very slowly. Sometimes stress builds up where plates push or slide past each other. When the rock suddenly slips, energy is released as **waves** that shake the ground. That shaking is an **earthquake**.

- Most earthquakes are small and not felt. Big ones can bring down buildings.
- We cannot stop earthquakes or predict exactly when they will come. But we can **build safely** and **prepare**.
- Earthquake strength is measured with an instrument called a **seismograph**.

In India, the Himalayan region, the north-east, Kutch and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands are among the areas that get stronger earthquakes.

keyTerms: Earthquake — sudden shaking of the ground
Plates — giant pieces of the Earth's outer layer
Seismograph — instrument that records earthquakes
Relief — help given after a disaster

check.q: What causes an earthquake?
options: Sudden slipping of rocks deep inside the Earth
check.why: When stressed rocks underground suddenly slip, they send out waves that shake the ground.

sections.md:
After the earthquake, the girl remembers how people **helped**:

- Neighbours dug through rubble with their bare hands to rescue people trapped under walls.
- The **army**, police, doctors, nurses and volunteers came from all over India and from other countries.
- People set up **relief camps** with tents. Trucks brought **food, water, blankets, medicines and clothes**. Children in faraway schools collected things to send.
- Hospitals were set up in tents because buildings were damaged.
- People of every religion and caste worked together, sharing food and shelter.

The chapter also talks about **feelings**: fear when the ground shakes again (aftershocks), sadness at losing loved ones, and how talking, playing together and going back to school helped children feel better.

check.q: What is a relief camp?
options: A place with tents, food and medicines for people who lost their homes
check.why: Relief camps give shelter, food, water and medical care to people affected by a disaster.

sections.md:
Slowly, villages were **rebuilt**. Engineers taught people how to make **earthquake-resistant houses**:

- Strong **foundations** and walls tied together with **bands of reinforced concrete** (at plinth, window/lintel and roof level).
- Light roofs that do not crush people if they fall.
- Following building rules for the area.

Interestingly, many traditional Kutchi **bhunga** houses — round mud huts with conical thatched roofs — survived well, because their round shape spread the shaking evenly.

Schools and hospitals were rebuilt to be safer. Today, Bhuj has a big museum and memorial, **Smritivan**, that remembers the earthquake and teaches about safety.

head: Unsafe
Safer
rows: Heavy stone roof on weak walls
Concrete bands at plinth, lintel and roof
Round bhunga shape, or tied frame
fig.caption: Making buildings safer.

sections.h: What to do in an earthquake
sections.md:
Remember: **Drop, Cover, Hold on**.

**Inside a building:**
1. **Drop** to the floor.
2. Take **cover** under a strong table or bed; protect your head and neck.
3. **Hold on** until the shaking stops.
4. Stay away from windows, glass, cupboards and things that may fall.
5. Do **not** use lifts; do not run on stairs while it is shaking.

**Outside:** move to an open space, away from buildings, trees, poles and electric wires.

**After:** check for injuries, go out calmly, listen to adults and the radio; there may be aftershocks.

**Emergency kit:** keep a bag with water, dry food, torch, first-aid kit, medicines, a whistle, copies of important papers and phone numbers. Schools hold **mock drills** to practise.

check.q: What should you do first indoors when an earthquake starts?
options: Drop, take cover under a strong table, and hold on
check.why: Drop, Cover and Hold on protects your head and body from falling objects during the shaking.

sections.h: Other disasters and how people cope
sections.md:
The chapter also looks at other disasters India faces:

- **Floods** — heavy monsoon rain makes rivers overflow (Assam, Bihar). People move to higher ground; boats bring help.
- **Cyclones** — strong storms from the sea hit coasts like Odisha, Andhra Pradesh and West Bengal. Warnings now help people move to cyclone shelters in time.
- **Tsunami** — giant sea waves after an undersea earthquake, as on **26 December 2004**, which hit Tamil Nadu and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
- **Droughts** and **landslides** too.

India has a **National Disaster Management Authority** and response teams (NDRF). Helpline numbers like **112** connect to emergency services.

> **Activity:** Collect newspaper reports about a disaster. Who helped? What did children do?

parts.md: After a school mock drill in Bhuj, Kiran packed an emergency bag with her mother: water bottles, biscuits, a torch, medicines and a small whistle. 'Why a whistle?' asked her little brother. 'If you're stuck, you can call without shouting yourself tired.'
Months later, a small tremor rattled the windows at night. Kiran didn't panic. 'Drop, cover, hold on!' She pulled her brother under the strong wooden bed until it stopped.
Outside in the open ground, neighbours gathered. Nothing was broken. Dadi hugged Kiran. 'In 2001 we didn't know these things. You children are teaching us.'

summary: On 26 January 2001 a strong earthquake struck Kutch, Gujarat (the Bhuj earthquake).
Earthquakes happen when rocks inside the Earth suddenly slip, sending out waves.
They cannot be stopped or exactly predicted, but we can prepare.
After the earthquake, neighbours, army, doctors and volunteers rescued and helped people.
Relief camps gave shelter, food, water, blankets and medicines.
Houses were rebuilt with concrete bands, strong foundations and light roofs.
Round bhunga huts of Kutch withstood shaking well.
In an earthquake: Drop, Cover, Hold on; outside, go to an open space.
Keep an emergency kit and practise mock drills.
India also faces floods, cyclones, tsunamis, droughts and landslides; NDMA and NDRF help.

rd-school-c5-evs-c.ch14-when-the-earth-s.title: When the Earth Shook! (part 2)
rd-school-c5-evs-c.ch14-when-the-earth-s.subtitle: Feelings after a disaster, emergency kits and helplines

sections.md:
In the chapter, children of Kutch in Gujarat talk about what the earthquake felt like: fear, losing their homes and school, and missing friends. Many lived in tents for months. Slowly, volunteers, the army, doctors and nearby villages brought food, water, blankets and medicines. Schools restarted in tents.

A disaster hurts minds as well as buildings. Children may have bad dreams or be scared of loud noises. Talking, drawing, playing together and getting back to a routine help people heal. Being kind and patient with someone who has lived through a disaster is a real way to help.

check.q: Which helps children recover after a disaster?
options: Talking, playing and returning to school
check.why: Sharing feelings and getting back to a normal routine helps people feel safe again.

sections.h: Be ready: an emergency kit and helplines
sections.md:
A family can keep an **emergency kit** in a bag near the door:

- drinking water and dry food (chana, biscuits)
- torch with extra batteries, a whistle
- first-aid box and needed medicines
- copies of important papers, some money
- a list of phone numbers

Practise a **mock drill** at school: on the signal, Drop, Cover, Hold; then walk out calmly to an open ground, away from buildings, trees and wires. Keep useful numbers: **112** (national emergency), **101** (fire), **108** (ambulance in many states).

**Activities:** Make a map of the safe open place near your school. Find out whether your area is in an earthquake-prone zone. Ask elders about any flood, cyclone or drought they remember and how people helped each other.
keyTerms: relief — help like food and shelter given after a disaster
mock drill — a practice of what to do in an emergency

check.q: Where should you go after shaking stops?
options: An open ground away from buildings and wires
check.why: Open ground has nothing that can fall on you if aftershocks come.

Disasters cause fear; talking and routine help healing.
Keep an emergency kit with water, food, torch, first aid.
Practise mock drills: Drop, Cover, Hold, then go to open ground.
Remember helplines like 112.

rd-school-c5-evs-c.ch15-blow-hot-blow-co.title: Blow Hot, Blow Cold
rd-school-c5-evs-c.ch15-blow-hot-blow-co.subtitle: The same breath warms your cold hands and cools your hot tea. How can that be?

sections.h: A puzzle on a winter morning
sections.md:
The chapter begins with a funny folk tale. A traveller in winter is given shelter. He blows on his cold hands — *'to warm them'*, he says. Later he blows on his hot food — *'to cool it'*, he says. His host is amazed and even a little scared: 'This man blows hot and cold from the same mouth!'

Then we meet children doing the same thing in class. One blows on her fingers on a chilly morning; another blows on a hot cup of tea. Both work. How?

The answer has to do with **how** we blow and with the **air** coming out of our body. Let's experiment.

sections.h: Experiment 1: hot breath and cold breath
sections.md:
Hold your palm close to your mouth.

1. Open your mouth wide and **breathe out slowly** — 'haaah' — as if fogging a mirror. Your palm feels **warm**.
2. Now make a small 'O' with your lips and **blow hard and fast** — 'phooo'. Your palm feels **cool**.

Why?
- The air coming from inside our body is **warm** (our body is about 37 °C). When we breathe out gently with an open mouth, this warm air reaches the hand directly — so it warms.
- When we blow fast through narrow lips, the moving air pulls along surrounding cooler air and moves quickly over the skin. Fast-moving air also helps **evaporation** of moisture from the skin or the tea, and evaporation **takes away heat**. So it feels cool.

Blowing on hot tea moves away the hot steam and speeds up evaporation, so the tea cools faster.

check.q: Why does fast blowing on hot tea cool it?
options: Moving air carries away steam and speeds evaporation, which removes heat
check.why: Fast-moving air removes hot vapour and speeds evaporation, and evaporation takes heat away from the tea.

sections.h: Experiment 2: the mist on the mirror
sections.md:
Breathe slowly on a cold mirror, a steel glass or your spectacles. A **mist** forms, then slowly disappears.

- Our breath contains **water vapour** (invisible). When it touches a cold surface, it cools and turns into tiny drops — that is the mist. This is **condensation**.
- The mist vanishes as the drops **evaporate** back into the air.

On very cold mornings you can even **see your breath** as a little cloud. In some hill towns, children play 'dragon' by puffing it out!

Also try: breathe on the mirror once with your mouth and once through your nose. Is there a difference?
keyTerms: Condensation — water vapour turning into drops on a cold surface
Evaporation — water turning into vapour
Exhale — breathe out
Inhale — breathe in

check.q: What is the mist on a mirror made of when you breathe on it?
options: Tiny drops of water from your breath
check.why: Water vapour in breath cools on the mirror and condenses into tiny water drops.

sections.h: Air that pushes: balloons, whistles and music
sections.md:
When we blow, we push **air**, and air can do work!

- **Balloons:** Blow into a balloon — it swells because air is pushed inside and presses on its walls. Let it go and the escaping air shoots it around the room.
- **Whistles and pressure horns:** blown air makes a sound.
- **Musical instruments:** the **flute (bansuri)**, **shehnai**, **conch (shankh)** and **harmonium** all use moving air. The air inside vibrates and we hear music. Blowing harder or covering holes changes the sound.
- **Toys:** a paper whirligig spins when blown; a straw can blow a paper ball across a table.

**Bottle challenge:** put a small paper ball just inside the mouth of an empty bottle lying on its side. Try blowing it **into** the bottle. Surprise — it flies **out** at you! The bottle is already full of air, and your blowing pushes air in which then rushes out, carrying the ball.

check.q: Which instrument makes music using blown air?
check.why: In a flute, blown air vibrates inside the tube to make musical sounds.

sections.h: Air pressure all around: dropper, pump and straw
sections.md:
The chapter's last part shows that air **presses** on everything.

- **Dropper:** Squeeze the rubber bulb (air goes out), dip it in water and let go — water rises inside, pushed up by the air outside.
- **Drinking straw:** When you suck, you remove air inside the straw; the air pressing on the drink pushes it up into your mouth.
- **Bicycle pump:** pushing the handle forces air into the tyre, making it hard and bouncy. Your hand feels the pump getting warm.
- **Cupping a glass:** fill a glass to the brim, put a postcard on top, turn it over carefully — the card stays, held by air pressure (try over a basin!).

And **breathing** itself: our **lungs** expand to pull air in through the nose, and squeeze to push it out. The nose has tiny hairs that filter dust, and it warms the air before it reaches the lungs.

story.title: The Guest Who Blew Two Ways

parts.md: One foggy evening, a tired traveller knocked at a farmer's hut in the hills. Shivering, he cupped his hands and blew on them. 'Why do you do that?' asked the farmer's son. 'To warm my fingers,' he said.
Dinner was steaming rice and dal. The traveller blew on his spoon. 'Now why?' 'To cool it.' The boy's eyes widened. 'Warm and cool from the same mouth? Are you a magician?'

Years later, that boy, now a science teacher, told the story to his class and then said, 'Let's test it.' Thirty palms went up to thirty mouths: haaah, phooo. Thirty faces grinned. The magic had a reason.

summary: We can blow warm air (slow, open mouth) or cool air (fast, narrow lips).
Air from our body is warm, about body temperature.
Fast-moving air speeds evaporation, which takes heat away — so blowing cools tea.
Breathing on a cold mirror forms mist by condensation of water vapour.
Blown air fills balloons, spins whirligigs and makes music in flutes and conches.
A paper ball blown at a bottle's mouth flies out because the bottle is full of air.
Air presses on everything: droppers, straws and pumps work because of air pressure.
Lungs pull air in and push it out; the nose filters and warms the air.
practice: How can we make our breath feel warm or cool on our palm?
Why do we blow on hot food?
Why does a mirror become misty when we breathe on it?
Name three musical instruments that use blown air.
What happens when you blow a paper ball into an empty bottle? Why?
How does a dropper take in water?
How does a straw help us drink?
Why is it better to breathe through the nose?

rd-school-c5-evs-c.ch15-blow-hot-blow-co.title: Blow Hot, Blow Cold (part 2)
rd-school-c5-evs-c.ch15-blow-hot-blow-co.subtitle: Why blowing cools soup, a folktale, and lungs at work

sections.md:
The chapter begins with an old folktale. A traveller blows on his cold hands to warm them, then blows on his hot food to cool it. His surprised host thinks he must be magic! Science explains it.

- When you breathe out with your **mouth wide open** ("haaa"), the air comes out slowly and is close to body temperature — warmer than cold hands. So hands feel warm.
- When you blow with **lips pushed into a small round shape** ("phoo"), the air rushes out fast. Fast-moving air pushes away the hot, wet air sitting on the soup and helps water evaporate. Evaporation takes heat away, so the food cools.

Same idea: a fan does not make the air colder, but moving air carries heat and sweat away from our skin, so we feel cool.

check.q: Blowing quickly on hot tea cools it mainly because…
options: moving air carries away heat and speeds evaporation
check.why: Fast air removes the warm moist layer and makes water evaporate faster, and evaporation takes heat.

sections.h: Our lungs: the pump inside us
sections.md:
Every blow starts in the **lungs**. When we breathe in, the chest gets bigger and air rushes in through the nose; when we breathe out, the chest gets smaller and air is pushed out. Try it: put your hand on your chest and count your breaths in one minute while sitting, then after running on the spot. You will breathe faster after exercise because your body needs more air.

**Activities from the chapter:** Make a whistle from a leaf or the cap of a pen. Blow into bottles filled with different amounts of water and listen to the different notes. Use a straw to blow bubbles in water — watch the air push the water. Find musical instruments played by blowing: flute (bansuri), shehnai, conch (shankh), harmonium (air from bellows).

**Did you know?** A grown-up at rest breathes about 12–20 times a minute.

check.q: Which instrument is played by blowing?
check.why: The bansuri sounds when blown air vibrates inside its hollow tube.

summary: Open-mouth breath is warm and slow; it warms hands.
Fast, narrow blowing cools food by removing heat and speeding evaporation.
A fan cools us by carrying heat and sweat away.
Lungs push air in and out; we breathe faster after exercise.
Blown air makes music in flutes, shehnai and conches.
practice: Explain how the same breath can warm hands and cool food.
Why do we feel cool under a fan?
Count your breaths before and after running. What changed and why?
Name three instruments played by blowing.
What happens when you blow through a straw into water?
Retell the folktale of the traveller in your own words.

rd-school-c5-evs-c.ch16-who-will-do-this.title: Who will do this Work?
rd-school-c5-evs-c.ch16-who-will-do-this.subtitle: Who sweeps the street, cleans the drain, washes the toilet? And why should every job get equal respect?

sections.md:
Think of your day. Who swept the road outside before you woke up? Who collected the garbage? Who cleaned the school toilets, cooked the mid-day meal, washed the dishes at home?

The chapter asks us to notice **cleaning work** — work that is very important but often **not respected**. Many people who do it are paid little, are not thanked, and are sometimes looked down upon.

**Survey activity:** Make a list of all the cleaning work done in your home and school. For each, write who does it — mother, father, grandparent, sister, brother, you, a helper, a sweeper. Do boys and girls share it equally? Which work do people avoid?

| Work | Who does it at home? | Who does it at school? |
|---|---|---|
| Sweeping floors | | |
| Washing toilets | | |
| Washing dishes | | |
| Taking out garbage | | |

The chapter tells a story from **Mahatma Gandhi's** life. At his ashram (in South Africa, and later at **Sabarmati** in Ahmedabad), **everyone** had to do all kinds of work — cooking, spinning, farming and **cleaning toilets**. In those days toilets were not flush toilets; waste had to be removed by hand, and only people of certain castes were forced to do it.

Gandhiji believed no work is low. In one well-known incident, his wife **Kasturba** did not want to clean the chamber pot of a guest who was from a so-called 'low' caste. Gandhiji was very firm that in their home everyone must do this work, and they had a serious quarrel. Later Kasturba too came to share his belief.

Gandhiji also designed simpler, cleaner ways of disposing of waste and taught ashram members to clean their own toilets. He said that cleaning was as important as prayer.

> **Think:** Is it fair that only some people do the dirtiest work while others never do it?

check.q: What rule did Gandhiji follow at his ashram?
options: Everyone, including himself, did all work, even cleaning toilets
check.why: Gandhiji believed in the dignity of labour, so everyone at the ashram shared all work, including cleaning toilets.

sections.md:
Even today, in some places, people are made to clean **dry latrines** and **sewers** with their hands, often without gloves, masks or boots. This is called **manual scavenging**. It is dangerous — workers can fall sick or even die from poisonous gases in sewers — and it is deeply unfair, because for generations it was forced on people of certain castes.

The chapter tells the story of a man who grew up in a family of such workers and decided to fight for their dignity. He travelled across the country, met workers, collected facts and asked the government to stop this practice. The movement he helped build, the **Safai Karmachari Andolan**, works so that people can leave this work, get education for their children and find other jobs.

In India, employing people for manual scavenging is **against the law** (laws were passed in 1993 and again, more strongly, in 2013). Machines, protective gear and proper sewers should be used instead.
keyTerms: Dignity of labour — every honest work deserves respect
Manual scavenging — removing human waste by hand (banned by law)
Discrimination — treating people unfairly because of caste, gender, religion or work
Sanitation — safe disposal of waste and keeping places clean

check.q: Why is manual scavenging wrong?
options: It is unsafe, unhealthy and unfairly forced on certain groups; it is banned by law
check.why: Manual scavenging harms workers' health and dignity, was forced on particular castes, and is illegal in India.

sections.md:
In many homes, cleaning, cooking and washing are done mostly by **women and girls**, while boys and men do little. The chapter asks: is this fair?

- Work at home is real work, even if it is not paid.
- If everyone shares, it gets done faster and no one is tired out.
- Boys can sweep, wash dishes and fold clothes as well as girls.

The chapter also asks you to look at the people who come to help in houses — **domestic workers** who clean and cook for several families. How do people speak to them? Do they have proper breaks, water to drink, fair pay and a chair to sit on? Small things like saying **thank you**, using their name respectfully and not giving them separate utensils show respect.

fig.alt: Icons of four household chores with progress bars filling up one after another.

check.q: Which is the fairest way to share housework?
options: Everyone in the family shares it
check.why: When every family member shares housework, it is fair and no one is overburdened.

sections.md:
Clean surroundings prevent diseases like **diarrhoea, cholera and typhoid**, and stop mosquitoes and flies breeding.

What can we do?
1. Do not throw garbage on the road; use dustbins.
2. **Separate waste**: wet (food peels) and dry (paper, plastic).
3. Use toilets and keep them clean; wash hands with soap.
4. In school, take turns to clean the classroom — many schools do this every day.
5. Respect sanitation workers; thank them, and do not make their work harder.

The **Swachh Bharat Mission** (launched on 2 October 2014, Gandhiji's birthday) aims to build toilets and keep India clean.

> **Debate in class:** 'If everyone cleaned up after themselves, would we need anyone to clean for us?'

parts.md: In Class 5B in Lucknow, the teacher stuck up a duty chart: sweeping, dusting, watering plants, emptying the bin, cleaning the board. Arjun frowned. 'Sweeping is not my job. Bhaiya does it.'
The teacher smiled and told them about Gandhiji cleaning toilets at Sabarmati. Then she picked up a broom herself and started. The class went quiet. One by one, they joined in, Arjun too.
That afternoon, Ramesh Bhaiya, the school's cleaner, found the classroom shining. Arjun walked up and said, 'Thank you for doing this every day, Bhaiya. Now we know how hard it is.'

summary: Cleaning work is essential, but often not respected or fairly paid.
Survey who does each cleaning job at home and school.
At Gandhiji's ashram everyone did all work, including cleaning toilets.
Gandhiji believed in the dignity of labour — no work is low.
Manual scavenging means removing human waste by hand; it is dangerous, unfair and banned by law.
The Safai Karmachari Andolan works for the freedom and dignity of such workers.
Housework should be shared by everyone, not only women and girls.
Domestic workers deserve fair pay, rest and respect.
Clean surroundings prevent disease; segregate waste and use dustbins.
Swachh Bharat Mission began on 2 October 2014.

What is manual scavenging? Why has it been banned?
How can we show respect to people who clean our streets and schools?

rd-school-c5-evs-c.ch16-who-will-do-this.title: Who will do this Work? (part 2)
rd-school-c5-evs-c.ch16-who-will-do-this.subtitle: Bezwada Wilson, laws, and your own survey of work

sections.md:
The chapter tells how some people were forced, for generations, to clean dry toilets by hand and carry waste on their heads. **Bezwada Wilson**, who grew up in a family that did this work in Karnataka, started the **Safai Karmachari Andolan** to end it. He and his friends went from place to place helping workers leave the work, find other jobs and send children to school.

India has laws against it: the **1993 Act** banned dry latrines and manual scavenging, and a stronger law in **2013** also promised help to start new lives. Laws matter, but they work only when everyone builds proper toilets and treats every worker with respect.

check.q: What did the Safai Karmachari Andolan work for?
options: Ending manual scavenging and helping workers find new lives
check.why: The movement campaigns so nobody has to clean human waste by hand and workers get dignified jobs.

sections.h: Your survey: who does which work?
sections.md:
Do a survey at home and in your neighbourhood:

| Work | Who does it at home? | Who does it in school/street? |
|---|---|---|
| Sweeping | | |
| Washing toilets | | |
| Washing dishes | | |
| Collecting garbage | | |

Then think: Is the work shared between boys and girls, men and women? Are people who clean paid fairly and thanked? Would you sweep your classroom? Gandhiji believed **no work is low** — cleaning is as worthy as reading or teaching.

**Things to do:** Keep your own space clean. Never throw garbage on roads. Separate wet and dry waste. Greet and thank the sanitation workers on your street.
keyTerms: dignity — the respect every person deserves
manual scavenging — cleaning human waste by hand

check.q: What did Gandhiji believe about cleaning work?
options: Only some people should do it
No work is low; everyone should clean
Machines must do all of it
check.why: In his ashram everyone, including Gandhiji, cleaned toilets to show all work is equally respectable.

summary: Manual scavenging was forced on some communities for generations.
Bezwada Wilson led the Safai Karmachari Andolan.
Laws of 1993 and 2013 ban it.
No work is low; share chores at home.
Respect and thank sanitation workers; keep surroundings clean.

Why is manual scavenging wrong?
Fill in a survey of who does cleaning work in your home.
Should cleaning be shared by boys and girls? Give reasons.
List three ways you can keep your street clean.
What did Gandhiji teach about work in his ashram?

rd-school-c5-evs-c.ch17-across-the-wall.title: Across the Wall
rd-school-c5-evs-c.ch17-across-the-wall.subtitle: A team of girls, a basketball court and many walls — some of brick, some in people's minds.

sections.h: A team that would not give up
sections.md:
The chapter is the true-to-life account of a **girls' basketball team** from a neighbourhood in **Delhi**. Told in a girl player's voice, it shows how a group of ordinary schoolgirls learnt a new game, faced many objections, and went on to play — and win — matches in other places.

Why is it called *Across the Wall*? At first the girls watched boys playing on a court on the other side of a wall. Girls playing outside was something many grown-ups around them did not accept. Slowly, the team climbed over many 'walls': fear, teasing, family worries, and the belief that 'sports are only for boys'.

(Read the full chapter in the official textbook — link at the end. Here is a retelling in our own words.)

The girls joined a sports programme run in their area. In the beginning:

- Some **families did not want** them to go out to play. They worried what neighbours would say, or wanted the girls to help at home.
- Some **boys teased** them, saying girls are too weak for basketball.
- The girls did not have proper shoes or clothes for the game. Some played in salwar kameez and chappals!
- They had to finish housework and studies first, then rush to practice.

Their **coach** talked to parents, explaining that sports make children healthy, confident and disciplined. A few parents came to watch — and changed their minds when they saw how hard the girls worked.

> **Think:** Are there games that people say are only for boys or only for girls where you live? Why do they say so?

check.q: What was one problem the girls faced at the start?
options: Families worried and some boys teased them
They had too much free time
check.why: Many families did not want girls to play outside, and boys teased them, so the team had to overcome these walls.

sections.md:
**Basketball** is played by two teams of **five** players on a court. Each team tries to throw the ball through the other team's **basket** — a ring with a net, about **3.05 metres** (10 feet) high.

- You move the ball by **dribbling** (bouncing it while you walk or run) or **passing** to a teammate.
- You cannot run holding the ball; that is a foul.
- A basket usually scores **2 points**; from far outside the arc, **3 points**; a free throw, **1 point**.

The girls practised dribbling, passing, shooting and running every day. They learnt that basketball needs **teamwork**: one player cannot win alone. Passing to the free player matters more than showing off.

They also learnt to be fit: warm-ups, stretching, eating well, drinking water and sleeping on time.

keyTerms: Dribble — bounce the ball while moving
Pass — throw the ball to a teammate
Foul — breaking a rule of the game
Teamwork — working together for a shared goal

check.q: How many players does each basketball team have on court?
check.why: Each basketball team has five players on the court at a time.

sections.md:
As they got better, the team went to play **matches** in other parts of the city and later in other places. For many girls it was their **first trip** away from home without their parents, their first time on a train or in a hostel.

They lost some games and cried. The coach told them that losing teaches you what to practise. They kept trying, and started to **win**. Medals and certificates came home, and the same neighbours who had criticised them began to praise them.

The girls also made friends with players from **different backgrounds and communities**. On the court, it didn't matter whose family was rich or poor, or which religion they followed: everyone was a teammate. The 'wall' between people also came down.

check.q: What did the coach say about losing a match?
options: Losing teaches you what to practise
check.why: Losses show what needs improvement, so the team learnt from them and practised harder.

sections.h: Indian women who broke walls in sport
sections.md:
Many Indian women have shown that sports are for everyone:

- **P. T. Usha** — the 'Payyoli Express', a sprinter who just missed an Olympic medal in 1984.
- **Karnam Malleswari** — weightlifter; first Indian woman to win an Olympic medal (bronze, Sydney 2000).
- **M. C. Mary Kom** — boxer from Manipur; six-time world champion and Olympic bronze medallist (2012).
- **Saina Nehwal** and **P. V. Sindhu** — badminton Olympic medallists.
- **Mithali Raj** — longtime captain of India's women's cricket team.
- Hockey, kabaddi, wrestling and football teams of Indian women also win international medals.

Many of them came from small towns and faced their own walls of money, comments and lack of facilities.

> **Activity:** Find a newspaper photo of a sportswoman. Paste it in your notebook and write three things about her.

The chapter ends by asking what games you play, where, and with whom:

- Is there a playground near your home? Do girls use it as much as boys?
- Are there games children with **disabilities** can play too? (Wheelchair basketball and the **Paralympics** show they can!)
- What traditional games do your grandparents remember — gilli-danda, kho-kho, kabaddi, pithoo (lagori), stapu?

Sport teaches **teamwork, fair play, discipline, confidence and friendship**. Every child has the right to play.

parts.md: Salma used to sit on the low wall watching boys play. 'Come play,' said the new coach one day. 'Girls?' laughed a boy. Salma went home and asked Ammi, who hesitated, then said, 'Only after homework.'

For weeks, her shots missed. Her chappals slipped. Then her team pooled money for second-hand shoes. One evening, she dribbled past two players and the ball dropped clean through the net. Her team screamed.
At the inter-zone final, Ammi sat in the crowd for the first time. When the medals were given, Salma ran straight to the stands. 'Ammi, we climbed over the wall!'

summary: The chapter is a girl's account of a girls' basketball team in Delhi.
The 'walls' were family worries, teasing, lack of kit and the idea that sports are for boys.
A coach and supportive parents helped the girls keep playing.
Basketball: five players a side; dribble, pass and shoot at a basket about 3.05 m high.
Baskets score 2 or 3 points; free throws score 1.
Teamwork and fitness matter more than one star player.
The team travelled, lost, learnt and began to win.
Sport brings together children of different backgrounds.
Indian sportswomen like P. T. Usha, Karnam Malleswari and Mary Kom broke many barriers.
Every child, including children with disabilities, has the right to play.

rd-school-c5-evs-c.ch17-across-the-wall-.title: Across the Wall (part 2)
rd-school-c5-evs-c.ch17-across-the-wall-.subtitle: Basketball rules, fitness and the chapter's discussion questions

sections.md:
The girls in the chapter play **basketball**. Two teams of **five players** each try to throw the ball through the other team's hoop, a ring about **3 metres (10 feet)** high. You move the ball by **dribbling** (bouncing it while walking or running) or by **passing** it to a teammate. You may not run while holding the ball. A basket usually scores **2 points**, and a long shot from beyond the arc scores **3**; a free throw scores 1.

Basketball needs speed, sharp eyes and above all **teamwork** — a player who never passes cannot win alone.

check.q: How many players does each basketball team have on the court?
check.why: Each side plays with five players at a time.

sections.md:
The 'wall' in the title is not only the wall of the school ground. It is the wall of ideas like *girls should stay home* or *sport is for boys*. The girls crossed it with practice, support from a coach and their families, and by proving themselves in matches.

Playing games also builds a **healthy body** (strong heart, lungs and muscles) and a **healthy mind** — learning to lose gracefully, to try again, and to trust friends.

**Talk about it:** Do girls and boys in your school get the same time on the playground? Which games are played in your area? Has anyone stopped you from doing something because of being a girl or a boy? Make a list of Indian sportswomen you know — like Mary Kom (boxing), P. V. Sindhu (badminton), Mithali Raj (cricket) — and what they won.

check.q: What does the 'wall' in the title stand for?
options: Ideas that stop girls from playing
check.why: The girls had to cross the barrier of beliefs that sport was not for them.

summary: Basketball: five players a side, hoop about 3 m high.
Dribble and pass; baskets score 2 or 3 points.
Teamwork wins games.
The 'wall' is unfair ideas about girls and sport.
Sport builds a healthy body and mind.
Everyone should get equal chances to play.

rd-school-c5-evs-c.ch18-no-place-for-us.title: No Place for Us?
rd-school-c5-evs-c.ch18-no-place-for-us.subtitle: When a dam is built, a village goes under water. Where do its people go?

sections.md:
Imagine a village by a river. Your family has farmed there for generations; your grandmother's grandmother was born there. There's a big banyan tree where you play, a temple, a weekly haat. One day an officer comes and says: *'A big dam will be built downstream. The water will rise and this village will be under the reservoir. You must move.'*

This really happens. When large **dams** are built, the water stored behind them floods huge areas, including villages, forests and farms. The families who must leave are called **displaced people**.

This chapter tells the story of such a family, told by a boy, Jadav — how they had to move to a city, what life there was like, and why they sometimes felt there was *no place* for them. We'll explore:

- the boy's story and his memories of the village
- why dams are built and who benefits
- what displacement means for families
- life for migrants in cities
- what is fair: rehabilitation and rights
- activities: talk, find out, survey and think

The chapter is written like a boy speaking to us. Here it is, retold in our own words.

**Scene 1 – Memories.** The boy remembers his village in the hills by the river. The family grew millets and maize, kept goats and a cow, picked fruits, leaves and medicines from the forest, and fished in the river. Festivals were celebrated together. Nobody needed to buy much; the forest and river gave a lot.

**Scene 2 – The news.** Officers came and said a dam was coming and the village would be under water. The elders went to meetings, signed papers they could not fully read, and waited. Some families got money; others were told their land was not 'recorded'.

**Scene 3 – The water rises.** One monsoon the water climbed higher and higher. Fields, then houses, then the old tree went under. The family carried what they could.

**Scene 4 – The city.** They reached a big city. Father found work carrying bricks at building sites; mother cleaned houses. They lived in a small hut in a crowded settlement. The boy missed the river and the open sky. He went to school sometimes, and worked sometimes.

**Scene 5 – Fear again.** One day there was news that the settlement would be broken because a new road was coming. The boy asks: *we were moved for a dam; now we are moved for a road — is there no place for us?*

The meaning: the people who make way for 'development' often get the least from it. For the exact text, read the free official chapter (link at the end).

check.q: Why does the boy feel there is 'no place' for his family?
options: They were moved for a dam and now may be moved again in the city
They do not like the city
check.why: His family lost their village to a dam and now face eviction from the city settlement too, so they feel unwanted everywhere.

sections.md:
Dams are huge walls across rivers. They:

- store water for **irrigation** (watering crops) in dry areas
- give **drinking water** to towns and cities
- make **electricity** (hydroelectric power) when water rushes through turbines
- help control **floods**

India has built many large dams — **Bhakra Nangal** (Sutlej), **Hirakud** (Mahanadi), **Tehri** (Bhagirathi), and **Sardar Sarovar** on the **Narmada**. They have helped grow food and light homes for crores of people.

But the reservoir behind a dam can cover hundreds of villages. People living there — often farmers, fisherfolk and **Adivasi** (tribal) communities who depend on the forest — lose their land, homes and way of life.

The **Narmada Bachao Andolan**, a movement led by people including **Medha Patkar**, has spoken up since the 1980s for the rights of families affected by the Narmada dams.

keyTerms: Dam — a wall built across a river to store water
Reservoir — the lake formed behind a dam
Displaced — forced to leave one's home
Rehabilitation — helping displaced people settle and earn again

check.q: Which of these is NOT a use of dams?
check.why: Dams store water for irrigation, drinking and electricity and help control floods — they don't change mountains.

sections.md:
Here are some big dams you may hear about. Find them on a map of India.

Notice that each dam is on a river that flows through hills or forests — the very places where Adivasi and farming villages are found. That is why big dams so often mean big displacement.

> **Did you know?** Some people suggest many **small check-dams** and rain-water ponds instead of a few giant dams. They store water near villages and displace almost nobody.

head: Dam
River
State
fig.caption: Some large dams of India.

sections.md:
Let's follow one family from a village by the Narmada — father, mother, grandmother and two children.

They are told they'll get some **compensation** (money) or land elsewhere. But:

- the money is not enough to buy as much land as they had
- the new land offered is far away, stony, or already used by others
- the papers take years; some people are left out because their land was never written in records
- the village community is **scattered** — neighbours end up in different places
- they lose their **forest**, river, fishing, festivals at the old temple

The grandmother keeps asking, 'Where will my bones rest, if not in my village?'

With little choice, the father goes to a **city** to look for work. Later the family joins him. They are now **migrants**.

check.q: Why do some displaced families get no land or money?
options: Their land was never written in official records
check.why: Families without official land papers, often Adivasis and the poor, may be left out of compensation.

sections.md:
In the city, the family has no house. They build a small **jhuggi** (hut) of tin, plastic and bricks in a **slum** near a drain or railway line, because that's the only space they can find. The father works as a **daily-wage labourer** at construction sites — some days there's work, some days none. The mother works as a domestic helper.

Problems they face:

- **No clean water** — long queues at a single tap or tanker
- **No toilets** nearby
- Children may not get a school seat, or must drop out to earn
- Fear that the **bulldozers** will come and break their huts because they're on 'government land'
- People calling them 'outsiders'

And yet these workers **build our cities** — our flats, roads, metros and malls. So the question in the chapter's title is really asked to *us*: *Is there no place for them?*

check.q: Why do many displaced families end up living in city slums?
options: They cannot afford other housing and need work
The government gives them flats immediately
check.why: With little money and an urgent need for work, slums near jobs are often the only place they can live.

sections.md:
Development like dams, roads and factories is needed. But it must be **fair** to the people who pay the price.

- **Ask** the affected people before deciding, and listen to them.
- Give **land for land**, of good quality, near each other so communities stay together.
- Make sure the new places have **schools, water, health centres and roads** before people move.
- Help them learn **new skills** and get jobs.
- In cities, give migrants **ration cards, schooling, and decent low-cost housing**.

India's 2013 land law (LARR Act) includes rules for **rehabilitation and resettlement** when land is acquired. Courts, including the Supreme Court, have also heard cases about the Narmada families.

> **Think:** If your school had to move to make way for a new road, what would you want the planners to do for you?

check.q: Which is a fair way to resettle displaced villagers?
options: Give them a little money and forget them
Give land for land, keep communities together and provide schools and water
Send each family to a different state
Ask them to wait for 20 years
check.why: Good-quality land, communities kept together and basic services help displaced families rebuild their lives.

sections.md:
The chapter asks you to look around you. Try these:

**Talk about it**
- Has your family, or anyone you know, ever had to move from one place to another? Why? What did they miss?
- What would you take with you if you had only one hour to leave your home?

**Find out**
- Who builds the buildings and roads in your area? Where have they come from?
- Is there a settlement of migrant workers near you? Do the children there go to school?

**Survey** (in groups, politely, with an adult)
Ask three workers: Where is your home village? Why did you come here? Where do you get water? What do you miss most? Put the answers in a table and share in class.

**Write**
Imagine you are the boy. Write a letter to a friend still in the village, describing the city.

> **Did you know?** Crores of Indians are migrants inside their own country. Many go home for festivals like Chhath, Holi or Pongal — the trains are packed!

summary: The chapter is the story of a boy whose village was drowned by a dam reservoir.
Big dams store water for irrigation, drinking, electricity and flood control.
The reservoir behind a dam can flood many villages, forests and farms.
People forced to leave are called displaced people.
Sardar Sarovar on the Narmada is one well-known dam; the Narmada Bachao Andolan spoke for affected families.
Compensation is often not enough, delayed, or missed by those without land papers.
Displaced families often migrate to cities for work.
In cities they may live in slums with poor water, toilets and fear of eviction.
Migrant workers build and run our cities.
Fair development means consulting people, giving land for land and proper resettlement.
Small check-dams can store water with little displacement.
practice: Why are big dams built? Give four reasons.
What happens to villages when a dam reservoir fills?
Who are displaced people?
Why do some families not get proper compensation?
Describe the problems faced by a migrant family in a city slum.
Name two big dams in India and their rivers.
What would be a fair way to help people displaced by a dam?
Imagine you are the boy in the story. Write what you miss about your village.
Do you think migrants have a place in our cities? Give reasons.

rd-school-c5-evs-d.ch19-a-seed-tells-a-f.title: A Seed tells a Farmer's Story
rd-school-c5-evs-d.ch19-a-seed-tells-a-f.subtitle: Three generations of one farming family — and how a tiny seed changed their lives.

sections.md:
In a farmer's house in Gujarat sits an old earthen pot. Inside, wrapped in cloth and mixed with neem leaves and ash, are seeds — bajra, jowar, moong, til. 'These came from my father's fields,' says the grandfather. 'And his father's before that.'

His grandson, now a farmer himself, buys seeds in shiny packets from the market. The two often argue about the best way to farm.

In this chapter, a seed tells the story of how farming changed over three generations:

- how farming was done in grandfather's time
- the big changes of the 1960s onwards
- benefits and problems of new methods
- money, loans and the farmer's worries
- how farmers today are combining old and new
- activities: talk to a farmer, find out, think

In grandfather's youth, farming went like this:

- **Seeds** were saved from the best plants of the harvest and stored in pots with neem leaves or ash to keep insects away. Families **exchanged** seeds with neighbours.
- **Many crops** were grown together or in turns — millets, pulses, oilseeds, vegetables. This is called **mixed cropping** and **crop rotation**, and it kept the soil healthy. Pulses add nitrogen to soil.
- **Manure** came from cow dung and leaves.
- **Bullocks** pulled the plough; water came from wells (lifted by bullocks with a *kos* or *charas*) and rain.
- Insects were controlled with **neem**, ash and birds.
- Farm work was shared — families helped each other at harvest.

Yields (amount of crop per field) were **lower**, and in bad years there could be hunger. But costs were also low, and the soil stayed rich.

check.q: Why did farmers store seeds with neem leaves?
check.why: Neem keeps insects away, so the stored seeds stay healthy until sowing time.

sections.md:
Farming follows the seasons. In most of India there are two main crop seasons.

The farmer's work in each season goes in steps: **ploughing** the soil, **sowing** seeds, **watering**, **weeding**, protecting from pests, **harvesting**, **threshing** (separating grain), and finally **storing** or **selling**. Grandfather did most steps by hand or with bullocks. His grandson uses a tractor, a pump, and sometimes a hired harvester machine.

> **Did you know?** Many Indian festivals are harvest festivals — Baisakhi in Punjab, Pongal in Tamil Nadu, Bihu in Assam, Makar Sankranti and Lohri in many states.

head: Season
Sown
Harvested
Example crops
rows: Rice, bajra, jowar, maize, cotton, moong
fig.caption: The two main crop seasons of India.

check.q: Which crop is a rabi (winter) crop?
check.why: Wheat is sown in winter (Oct–Nov) and harvested in spring, so it is a rabi crop.

sections.md:
In the **1960s**, India faced food shortages and had to bring in grain from other countries. Scientists like **M. S. Swaminathan** (and the American scientist Norman Borlaug, who developed the dwarf wheat) helped introduce **high-yielding varieties (HYV)** of wheat and rice. Along with these came:

- **chemical fertilisers** (urea, DAP)
- **pesticides** to kill insects
- **tubewells** and pumps for irrigation
- **tractors** and machines

Wheat and rice harvests grew enormously, especially in **Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh**. India became able to feed itself. This was called the **Green Revolution**.

The grandson's father switched to these methods. For some years, his fields gave **much more** grain, and the family's income rose.

fig.alt: A line graph that rises slowly till 1965 and then steeply upward to 2020.

keyTerms: High-yielding variety — seed that gives much more grain
Fertiliser — substance added to soil to help plants grow
Pesticide — chemical to kill insect pests
Green Revolution — big rise in food production from the 1960s

check.q: What was the Green Revolution?
options: A big rise in food production using new seeds, fertilisers and irrigation
check.why: From the 1960s, high-yielding seeds, fertilisers and irrigation greatly increased wheat and rice harvests.

sections.md:
After many years, the family noticed troubles:

- **Soil got tired**: using only chemical fertilisers year after year made the soil hard and less fertile. More and more fertiliser was needed for the same crop.
- **Water ran low**: tubewells pumped up so much groundwater that wells had to be dug deeper and deeper.
- **Pests became stronger**: insects stopped dying from the usual pesticides, so stronger ones were used — harming birds, earthworms, bees and sometimes farmers' health.
- **New seeds every year**: many modern seeds don't give good crops if saved, so farmers must **buy** them each season.
- **Costs went up**: seeds, fertilisers, pesticides, diesel, electricity — all cost money. Many farmers took **loans**. If rain failed or prices fell, they couldn't repay.
- **Fewer crops**: many grew only wheat and rice; millets and pulses were grown less.

check.q: Why did many farmers need loans after switching to new methods?
options: Seeds, fertilisers and pesticides cost a lot
check.why: Buying seeds, fertilisers, pesticides and fuel each season raised costs, so many farmers borrowed money.

sections.md:
Let us do a simple sum, the way the grandson does in his notebook. Suppose for one field he spends ₹4,000 on seeds, ₹6,000 on fertiliser, ₹3,000 on pesticide and ₹5,000 on diesel and electricity. Total cost = 4,000 + 6,000 + 3,000 + 5,000 = **₹18,000**.

If the crop is good and he sells it for ₹30,000, he keeps ₹30,000 − ₹18,000 = **₹12,000** for months of hard work. But if the rain fails and he sells only ₹15,000 worth, he **loses** ₹3,000 — and if he borrowed the ₹18,000 from a moneylender at high interest, the debt grows.

This is why farmers worry about rain, prices and loans. Help such as **bank loans at low interest**, **crop insurance** and a **minimum support price** from the government makes a big difference.

> **Think:** Who decides the price of the wheat in your kitchen? How much of it reaches the farmer?

check.q: Costs ₹18,000, sales ₹30,000. What does the farmer earn?
check.why: Earnings = sales − costs = 30,000 − 18,000 = ₹12,000.

sections.h: Mixing the old and the new
sections.md:
Today, the grandson listens to his grandfather again. Many farmers across India are trying:

- **Organic / natural farming**: using compost, vermicompost (made by earthworms), cow-dung manure, neem sprays. **Sikkim** became India's first fully organic state (declared in 2016).
- **Seed banks**: villages and groups save and share **traditional seeds** suited to local soil and weather.
- **Millets are back**: bajra, jowar, ragi need less water. **2023** was celebrated as the **International Year of Millets**, at India's suggestion.
- **Drip irrigation**: pipes drip water at plant roots, saving lots of water.
- **Soil Health Cards**: the government tests soil and tells farmers which nutrients they need.
- **Crop insurance and fair prices**: schemes that protect farmers if crops fail.

The best farming takes the **wisdom of the old** and the **tools of the new**.

check.q: Which state was declared India's first fully organic state?
check.why: Sikkim was declared fully organic in 2016, farming without chemical fertilisers and pesticides.

sections.md:
**Talk to a farmer** (or an elder who once farmed): Which seeds did your family grow? Where did you keep them? Did you use fertilisers? What changed over the years?

**Find out**: Which crops grow near your town? Which are kharif and which are rabi? Which grains are in your kitchen today, and which state might they come from?

**Do**: Soak a few moong seeds overnight and keep them on wet cotton. Watch the sprouts for a week and draw them every day. Try keeping some seeds with neem leaves and some without in a jar for a month — which get insects?

**Make a seed collection**: paste different seeds (rajma, chana, til, rice, wheat, mustard) on a chart and label them.

parts.md: I am a bajra seed. I slept in Dada's clay pot through a hot summer, wrapped in neem, dreaming of rain. When the monsoon came, Dada's rough hand scattered me into soft, dark soil beside moong and til. We grew up as friends, and the moong fed the soil for us all.

Then came the years of shiny packets. My cousins in the packets grew tall and heavy, and everyone cheered. But the soil grew pale and the well grew deep. Dada's pot stayed in a corner, gathering dust.

This year, the grandson opened the pot. He sowed me on one corner of the field, with compost and drip pipes. 'Let's see who does better,' he said to Dada, smiling. I am growing now, and I can feel earthworms tickling my roots. I think the soil is happy again.

summary: Earlier, farmers saved their own seeds and stored them with neem or ash.
Mixed cropping and crop rotation kept the soil healthy; pulses add nitrogen.
Bullocks, cow-dung manure and wells/rain were used.
Kharif crops grow in the monsoon; rabi crops in winter.
In the 1960s, the Green Revolution brought high-yielding seeds, fertilisers, pesticides and irrigation.
M. S. Swaminathan played a key role; food production rose greatly.
Over time: soil became less fertile, groundwater fell and pests became resistant.
Farmers had to buy seeds every year; costs and loans rose.
Earnings = sales − costs; a bad year can mean a loss and debt.
Many farmers now try organic farming, compost and neem sprays; Sikkim is fully organic (2016).
Seed banks save traditional seeds; millets are being promoted (2023, Year of Millets).
Drip irrigation and Soil Health Cards help save water and fertiliser.

What is mixed cropping? Why is it useful?

What was the Green Revolution? Name two things it introduced.
Write three problems that came from heavy use of chemicals.
Why did many farmers fall into debt?
A farmer spends ₹12,500 and sells his crop for ₹20,000. How much does he earn?
What is organic farming?
How does drip irrigation save water?
