sections.h: Why a tree as the speaker? Personification explained
sections.md:
When a tree speaks, remembers and gives advice like a wise elder, the writer is using **personification** — giving human qualities to something that is not human. Calling the tree *Baba* (a respectful word for an old man or grandfather) makes us feel the tree is family.

Personification does three jobs:
- It makes facts friendly — learning that neem leaves keep insects away is more memorable when 'Baba' tells you himself.
- It builds **empathy** — if a tree can feel, we think twice before cutting it.
- It links generations — the old tree has watched grandparents and grandchildren play under it.

**Try it:** Write three sentences in which a banyan, a mango tree or the monsoon cloud speaks about itself. Example: *'I am the monsoon. Every June I travel thousands of kilometres just to fill your village pond.'*

> **Did you know?** Neem (*Azadirachta indica*) is native to the Indian subcontinent. Its seeds contain *azadirachtin*, a natural substance studied for keeping pests off crops.
keyTerms: personification — giving human qualities to non-human things
empathy — understanding and sharing another's feelings
azadirachtin — a natural compound in neem seeds that repels insects

sections.md:
Many Indian homes use neem in traditional ways. Learn these as **general knowledge**, not medical advice — always check with a doctor before using anything as medicine.

| Part of the tree | Traditional use |
|---|---|
| Twigs | *datun* — chewed to clean teeth |
| Dried leaves | kept in grain bins and between woollen clothes to keep insects away |
| Leaves in water | bathing water in some homes |
| Seed oil | used in organic farming to protect crops |
| Shade | cools courtyards, schools and village squares |

Neem is also hardy: it grows in dry places, stays green most of the year, and gives deep shade in hot summers. That is why it is planted along roads in states such as Rajasthan and Gujarat.

**Project:** Interview an elder at home about one tree in your area. Ask: How old is it? What happened under it? What is it used for? Make a one-page 'Tree Biography'.

rd-school-c6-english-a.ch08-what-a-bird-.subtitle: Shell, nest, leaves, sky: a tiny bird's idea of 'the whole world' grows with every step

sections.h: A hook: how big is your world?
sections.md:
When you were three, 'the world' was probably your home and the lane outside. At six, it was your school too. Now you know about other states, other countries, galaxies… Every time we learn, our world grows.

**What a Bird Thought** is a short, much-loved poem whose author is unknown (*anonymous*). It is an old nursery verse, long in the public domain. It shows this idea through the eyes of a baby bird. At each stage of its life the bird is *sure* it knows what the world is like — and each time it discovers it was wrong.

In this companion: warm-up, the full traditional text, a line-by-line explanation, the central idea, devices, language work, skills activities and exam help.

> **Did you know?** Bird eggshells come in many colours — blue, green, speckled brown. Blue-green colour in eggs comes from a natural pigment called *biliverdin*.
keyTerms: anonymous — by an unknown author
perspective — the way someone sees things from where they are

check.q: The poem shows the bird's idea of the world…
options: growing bigger as its experience grows
check.why: At every new stage the bird realises the world is larger than it had believed.

sections.md:
**1. Life cycle of a bird.** Put these in order: *the bird flies away; an egg is laid; the chick hatches; the chick grows feathers in the nest; the mother sits on the egg to keep it warm.* (Answer: egg laid → mother sits on it → chick hatches → grows feathers → flies away.)

**2. My world circles.** Draw four circles inside one another. Label the smallest *my home*, then *my street/colony*, then *my town*, then *my country*. Which circle did you know first?

**3. Discuss.** Have you ever been *very sure* about something and then found out you were wrong? (Many children think the moon follows the car!) How did you feel?

**4. Predict.** The title is *What a Bird Thought*. What might a bird think about the world while it is still inside its egg?

check.q: What comes right after the mother bird sits on the egg?
check.why: The mother keeps the egg warm until the chick is ready to hatch.

sections.md:
*This is the traditional public-domain version of the poem. The version printed in your textbook may differ slightly in a word or punctuation; follow your book in exams.*

> I lived first in a little house,
> And lived there very well;
> I thought the world was small and round,
> And made of pale blue shell.
>
> I lived next in a little nest,
> Nor needed any other;
> I thought the world was made of straw,
> And brooded by my mother.
>
> One day I fluttered from the nest
> To see what I could find.
> I said, 'The world is made of leaves,
> I have been very blind.'
>
> At length I flew beyond the tree,
> Quite fit for grown-up labours.
> I don't know how the world is made,
> And neither do my neighbours!

Read it aloud. Notice the bouncy beat (four beats, then three, in each pair of lines) and the rhymes *well/shell, other/mother, find/blind, labours/neighbours*.

check.q: What colour was the shell the bird thought was the whole world?
check.why: The first stanza says the world seemed 'small and round, and made of pale blue shell'.

sections.h: Line by line: what it means
sections.md:
**Stanza 1 — inside the egg.**
- *'I lived first in a little house'* — the 'house' is the egg. Calling it a house is a **metaphor**.
- *'And lived there very well'* — the chick was comfortable, warm and safe.
- *'I thought the world was small and round'* — it could only see the curved inside of the egg, so it believed that was everything.
- *'And made of pale blue shell'* — even the colour of the whole world seemed pale blue. Our ideas take the colour of our surroundings!

**Stanza 2 — in the nest.**
- *'I lived next in a little nest'* — after hatching, a new, bigger home.
- *'Nor needed any other'* — it was happy and wanted nothing more.
- *'I thought the world was made of straw'* — now everything it touches is straw, so the 'whole world' is straw.
- *'And brooded by my mother'* — 'to brood' means to sit over eggs or chicks to keep them warm. The bird thinks its mother covering the nest covers the whole world. A sweet, funny picture.

**Stanza 3 — among the leaves.**
- *'One day I fluttered from the nest / To see what I could find'* — curiosity makes it leave. 'Fluttered' shows weak, new wings.
- *'I said, "The world is made of leaves"'* — another confident statement.
- *'I have been very blind'* — it admits it was wrong before. But readers smile: it is still 'blind' to the bigger world.

**Stanza 4 — beyond the tree.**
- *'At length I flew beyond the tree'* — at last, a grown bird, it flies free.
- *'Quite fit for grown-up labours'* — ready for adult work: finding food, building a nest.
- *'I don't know how the world is made'* — the wisest line. Having seen the most, it now claims to know the least. This is **humility**.
- *'And neither do my neighbours!'* — a joke with a deep point: no one, not even other grown birds, knows everything.

check.q: What does 'brooded' mean in stanza 2?
check.why: To brood is for a parent bird to sit over eggs or chicks to keep them warm.

sections.md:
| Stage | Where the bird is | What it believes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | inside the egg | the world is small, round, pale-blue shell |
| 2 | in the nest | the world is straw, covered by mother |
| 3 | on the branches | the world is leaves |
| 4 | flying free | it doesn't know — and nor does anyone |

The pattern is: **small space → certainty → new experience → wider view**. In the first three stanzas the bird is certain. In the last, it gives up certainty — and that is when it is wisest.

check.q: What did the bird think the world was made of when it was in the nest?
check.why: In the nest everything around it was straw, so it believed the world was made of straw.

sections.md:
**1. Our view depends on where we stand.** The bird is not foolish; it judges by what it can see. Humans do the same.

**2. Learning widens the world.** Every new experience — a new book, a trip, a friend from another state — makes the 'circle' bigger.

**3. Humility.** At the end, the bird admits it doesn't know everything. Wise people say *'the more I learn, the more I realise how much I don't know.'*

**4. Growing up.** The stages mirror human life: home → school → town → the wider world.

**5. Link to nature.** The poem sits in Unit 3, *Nurturing Nature*, because it celebrates the natural life cycle of a bird and the wonder of the open natural world.

**A story from India with the same idea:** the old tale of the **frog in the well** (*kupamanduka*) — a frog who had never left its well insisted the well was the whole world, until a frog from the sea told him otherwise. The bird is the opposite: it keeps leaving its 'well' and learning.

> **Think about it:** Draw four circles for your own life: what was your 'whole world' at age 2, 6, 10 and now?

check.q: Which line best states the poem's message?
options: Our understanding is limited by our experience, and grows as we explore
check.why: The bird's changing belief shows how experience expands our understanding of the world.

sections.md:
**Repetition.** Stanzas 1–3 repeat the pattern *'I thought the world was…'* / *'The world is made of…'*. This creates rhythm and makes the stages easy to follow.

**Imagery and colour.** We 'see' the pale blue shell, the straw, the leaves. Colours and textures help the reader feel each stage.

**Metaphor.** The egg is a 'little house'.

**First-person speaker.** The bird itself speaks, so we share its surprise.

**Rhyme scheme.** In each stanza lines 2 and 4 rhyme: *abcb* (well/shell, other/mother, find/blind, labours/neighbours).

**Structure = growth.** Each stanza is a step outward — the form of the poem copies its meaning.

**Gentle humour and irony.** We know more than the bird, so its confident statements make us smile kindly. The last line is a punchline.
keyTerms: imagery — words that create pictures in the mind
stanza — a group of lines in a poem
irony — when the reader knows more than the speaker
rhyme scheme abcb — only lines 2 and 4 rhyme

check.q: What is the rhyme scheme of each stanza?
check.why: Only the second and fourth lines rhyme (well/shell), giving abcb.

sections.h: Let us learn: words and grammar
sections.md:
**Words:** *flutter* (move wings quickly and lightly), *brood* (sit over young to warm them), *at length* (finally, after a long time), *labours* (work), *blind* (here: unable to understand).

**Bird words:** *hatch, chick, fledgling* (young bird learning to fly), *nestling, beak, plumage, migrate*.

**Grammar — sequence words.** The poem moves in order: *first, next, one day, at length*. Use them when you retell any process: *First the egg is laid. Next…*

**Grammar — simple past.** *lived, thought, fluttered, said, flew*. Which are regular (-ed) and which irregular? (lived, fluttered — regular; thought, said, flew — irregular.)

check.q: Which word means 'finally, after a long time'?
check.why: 'At length' means eventually or after a long time.

sections.h: Let us listen, speak, write and explore
sections.md:
**Listening.** Listen to birdsong in the morning for five minutes. How many different calls can you hear? Try to name the birds (sparrow, myna, koel, crow, bulbul).

**Speaking — recitation.** Recite the poem in four voices: a soft, cosy voice for the egg; a sleepy voice for the nest; an excited voice for the leaves; a wise, amused voice for the last stanza.

**Writing — new poem.** Write 'What a Fish Thought' — bowl → pond → river → ocean — using the same four-stanza pattern and the rhyme scheme abcb.

**Writing — paragraph.** *'My world has grown.'* Describe how your idea of the world has changed since you were small.

**Explore.** Watch a nest (from a distance, without disturbing it!) or read about the life cycle of the house sparrow. Draw the stages.

> **Did you know?** House sparrows have declined in many Indian cities; 20 March is observed as World Sparrow Day.

**Q. Where was the bird at first and what did it think?** Inside its egg; it thought the whole world was small, round and made of pale blue shell.

**Q. List the stages of the bird's life in the poem.** Egg → nest → leaves/branches → flying beyond the tree.

**Q. What did the bird realise at the end?** That it does not know how the world is made — and neither does anyone else. The world is far bigger than it had thought.

**Q. Explain 'I have been very blind'.** The bird means it had been unable to see the truth before; ironically it is still 'blind' to the even larger world.

**Q. (Long) How is the bird like a child growing up?** Compare egg/home, nest/family, leaves/neighbourhood and school, sky/wider world; mention curiosity and humility.

summary: 'What a Bird Thought' is a short traditional poem by an unknown (anonymous) author.
A bird describes its idea of 'the world' at each stage of growing up.
In the egg it thinks the world is small, round and pale-blue shell.
In the nest it thinks the world is straw, brooded by its mother.
Among branches it thinks the world is leaves and says it has been 'blind'.
Flying free, it admits it doesn't know how the world is made — nor do its neighbours.
Message: our view is limited by experience; learning widens it.
The poem teaches humility and curiosity — the opposite of the frog in the well.
Devices: repetition, imagery, metaphor (egg = house), first-person voice, irony.
Rhyme scheme abcb in every stanza.
Sequence words: first, next, one day, at length.

rd-school-c6-english-a.ch08-what-a-bird-.title: What a Bird Thought — The World Keeps Getting Bigger (part 2)
rd-school-c6-english-a.ch08-what-a-bird-.subtitle: Poetic devices, the growing-world figure, and exam practice

sections.h: The poem's structure: a world in widening circles
sections.md:
The poem is built like rings in a pond. Each stage the bird lives through feels like *the whole world* — until it discovers something bigger:

1. **The shell** — snug, small, one colour all around.
2. **The nest** — straw, sky above, brothers and sisters close by.
3. **The leaves and branches** — green everywhere once it leaves the nest.
4. **Open flight** — the bird finally admits it does not know how big the world really is.

The repeated pattern (*I thought the world was…*) is called **refrain-like repetition**. It gives the poem rhythm and makes the final surprise stronger. The bird's mistakes are not foolish; each belief was true *for what it could see*. That is the poem's gentle humour and its wisdom.

sections.md:
- **First-person speaker:** the bird itself speaks, so we see through its eyes.
- **Rhyme:** lines end in matching sounds, giving a sing-song feel suited to a young bird.
- **Colour imagery:** each stage has a colour (pale shell, brown straw, green leaves), so we *see* the change.
- **Irony of the ending:** a grown bird, after confident statements, finally says it does not know — real knowledge begins with knowing your limits.

**Vocabulary:** *snug* (warm and cosy), *fledgling* (young bird learning to fly), *flutter* (flap wings quickly), *perch* (sit on a branch).

> **Did you know?** Many songbirds hatch blind and featherless. They leave the nest after about two weeks — a fast journey from shell to sky!
keyTerms: fledgling — a young bird just learning to fly
imagery — words that create pictures in the mind
irony — an outcome opposite to what was expected

check.q: What lesson does the ending suggest?
options: Knowing that we don't know everything is wise
check.why: The bird's final humble admission shows that growing up means discovering how much more there is to learn.

rd-school-c6-english-a.ch09-spices-that-.title: Spices that Heal Us — The Kitchen as a Treasure Chest
rd-school-c6-english-a.ch09-spices-that-.subtitle: Turmeric, ginger, pepper, cumin, cinnamon, cloves: what grandparents knew and science is studying

sections.h: A hook: the spice box on your shelf
sections.md:
Open the round steel *masala dabba* in an Indian kitchen and you'll find a little rainbow — yellow turmeric, brown cumin, black pepper, red chilli, green cardamom. Five hundred years ago, sailors from Europe risked dangerous voyages to reach India for exactly these treasures.

**Spices that Heal Us** is the last chapter of Unit 3, *Nurturing Nature*. It is written as a friendly **conversation** in which an elder explains to a child how common spices not only add flavour but have long been used in home remedies. The chapter links nature, food, tradition and health.

The chapter's text is protected, so we explain it in our own words. Read it in your Poorvi book (free at ncert.nic.in). This companion covers: warm-up, how the conversation is built, each spice and its uses, the science in simple words, more spices of India, the spice trade, safety, language notes, skills activities and exam help.

> **Important:** Home remedies are part of tradition and are being studied by scientists, but they are not a replacement for a doctor. For any illness, always see a doctor.
keyTerms: spice — a dried seed, fruit, root or bark used to flavour food
remedy — something that helps cure or ease an illness
masala dabba — the round spice box in Indian kitchens

check.q: In what form is the chapter mainly written?
options: a conversation between an elder and a child
check.why: An elder explains spices to a curious child through dialogue.

sections.md:
**1. Spice hunt.** With an adult's permission, look inside your kitchen's spice box. List every spice you find with its name in English and in your home language.

**2. Smell and guess.** In class, your teacher may pass around small closed jars. Smell (don't taste!) and guess: Which is cumin? Which is clove? Which is cardamom?

**3. Home remedies.** Ask a grandparent: *What do you give a child with a cold? A stomach ache? A cough?* Many answers will contain spices — haldi doodh, ginger-honey, ajwain water.

**4. Discuss.** Why do you think so many traditional remedies use kitchen spices? (They are cheap, always at hand, and generations have tried them.)

check.q: When smelling spices in class, you should…
options: smell carefully without tasting or touching eyes
check.why: Smelling gently is safe; spice powders can irritate eyes, skin and throat.

sections.md:
The chapter is a **dialogue**: an elder (such as a grandmother or grandfather) and a child talk in the kitchen or at home, perhaps when the child has a cold or is curious about cooking.

**The pattern:**
1. The child notices something — the elder adding a pinch of a spice, or giving a remedy.
2. The child asks *why*.
3. The elder explains the spice's name, how it tastes or smells, and how it helps.
4. The child reacts — surprised, amused, or with another question — which leads to the next spice.

**Why this works:** The child asks exactly the questions a reader would ask. The elder's answers are short and practical. Each spice gets its own 'turn' in the conversation, so the information is divided neatly.

**Tone:** warm, affectionate, a little playful. The elder is proud of family knowledge; the child is curious, sometimes doubtful. The chapter quietly shows **respect between generations**.

**Reading tip:** Make a two-column table while you read — *Spice* | *What the elder says it does* — and fill it in as each spice appears.

check.q: Why does the writer have the child ask questions?
options: Because the child's questions are the reader's questions, so information comes naturally
check.why: A curious child voices what readers wonder, so the facts arrive as answers.

sections.md:
| Spice | Part of the plant | Traditional use | What science says (simply) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Turmeric (haldi)** | rhizome | milk with turmeric for colds; paste on small cuts | contains *curcumin*, studied for anti-inflammatory and antiseptic effects |
| **Ginger (adrak)** | rhizome | ginger tea for cough, sore throat, nausea | good evidence it can reduce nausea |
| **Black pepper (kali mirch)** | dried berry | with honey for cough | contains *piperine*; helps the body absorb curcumin better |
| **Cumin (jeera)** | seed | jeera water for digestion | traditionally used for stomach comfort |
| **Cinnamon (dalchini)** | bark | in teas, sweets | studied for effects on blood sugar (more research needed) |
| **Cloves (laung)** | dried flower bud | on an aching tooth | contain *eugenol*, a mild natural numbing agent used in dentistry |
| **Carom (ajwain)** | seed | for gas, stomach ache | traditional digestive |

*Your chapter may describe a slightly different list — note the ones it mentions and what it says about each.*

**How to remember:** *Turmeric Gives Pepper Courage, Cinnamon Cures Aches* — T-G-P-C-C-C-A (turmeric, ginger, pepper, cumin, cinnamon, cloves, ajwain).

check.why: Curcumin is the yellow compound in turmeric studied for its anti-inflammatory properties.

sections.h: Which part of the plant? A spice detective
sections.md:
Spices come from **every part** of a plant. This surprises most readers.

| Plant part | Spices |
|---|---|
| Underground stem (rhizome) | turmeric, ginger |
| Seed | cumin, ajwain, mustard, fenugreek (methi), coriander, cardamom seeds |
| Fruit / berry | black pepper, chilli, cardamom pod, star anise |
| Bark | cinnamon |
| Flower bud | clove |
| Flower part | saffron (the thread-like stigma of the crocus flower) |
| Dried resin (sap) | asafoetida (hing) |
| Leaf | curry leaves, bay leaf (tej patta) |

**More spices of India:**
- **Cardamom (elaichi)** — the 'queen of spices', grown in the Western Ghats; used in chai and sweets.
- **Fenugreek (methi)** seeds — bitter; used in pickles and *sambar* powder.
- **Mustard (rai/sarson)** — tiny seeds that pop in hot oil for *tadka*.
- **Asafoetida (hing)** — a pinch in dal, traditionally for digestion.
- **Saffron (kesar)** — grown in Kashmir (Pampore); the costliest spice by weight because each flower gives only three threads.

options: each flower gives only three tiny threads, picked by hand
check.why: Huge numbers of flowers must be hand-picked to collect a small weight of saffron threads.

sections.h: The spice route: why the world came to India
sections.md:
Spices made India famous across the ancient world.

- **Malabar coast (Kerala)** was a great centre of the **black pepper** trade; pepper was so valued it was nicknamed 'black gold'.
- Traders from Arabia, Rome, China and Southeast Asia came to Indian ports such as **Muziris** (an ancient port on the Kerala coast).
- In **1498**, **Vasco da Gama** reached **Calicut (Kozhikode)** by sea from Portugal — partly to buy spices directly.
- Later the Dutch, the English and the French East India Companies all competed for the spice trade.

So the little pepper in your *rasam* has a big history!

> **Did you know?** India today is one of the world's largest producers, consumers and exporters of spices. The government's **Spices Board** is based in Kochi, Kerala.

Muziris on the Kerala coast flourishes as a spice port
Vasco da Gama reaches Calicut by sea
European trading companies compete for Indian spices
India is a leading spice producer and exporter

fig.caption: Spices shaped history.

check.why: Black pepper from the Malabar coast was so valuable in trade it was called 'black gold'.

sections.h: Themes and a word of caution
sections.md:
**Themes**
1. **Nature's gifts:** roots, bark, seeds and flowers of plants give us flavour and wellness.
2. **Traditional knowledge:** elders pass down practical wisdom; the chapter honours it.
3. **Science meets tradition:** modern researchers study why some remedies work — and which don't.
4. **Healthy habits:** home-cooked food with spices is part of a balanced lifestyle.
5. **Conversation between generations:** the young learn by asking.

**Link across the unit:** *Neem Baba* showed a whole tree as a 'village pharmacy'; *What a Bird Thought* showed wonder at nature's size; *Spices that Heal Us* brings nature right into the kitchen.

**Caution, kindly:** Spices are safe in food amounts, but large amounts can upset the stomach, and some people are allergic. Never put spice powders in eyes or deep wounds. Home remedies are for mild discomfort; for fever, serious pain or injury — see a doctor.

> **Think about it:** Interview a grandparent about one home remedy. Then look up what scientists say about it. Do they agree?

check.q: What is the sensible way to think about home remedies?
options: They are traditional aids for mild discomfort; serious illness needs a doctor
They are dangerous and should never be used
check.why: Spices can help in small ways, but proper medical care is needed for real illness.

sections.md:
**Dialogue punctuation:** *"Dadi, why do you add haldi to milk?" asked Aisha.* — Quotation marks enclose spoken words; the question mark stays inside. Start a new line for each new speaker.

**Words:** *aromatic* (sweet-smelling), *pungent* (sharp-tasting), *antiseptic* (prevents infection), *digestion*, *inflammation*, *rhizome* (underground stem — turmeric and ginger are rhizomes, not true roots!), *remedy*, *soothing*.

**Adjectives of taste:** sweet, sour, salty, bitter, spicy/hot, tangy, astringent.

**Countable and uncountable nouns:** *a clove, two cloves; a cardamom pod* (countable) vs *some turmeric, a pinch of salt, a spoonful of honey* (uncountable — we measure them). Useful measure words: *a pinch of, a teaspoon of, a cup of, a stick of (cinnamon)*.

**Imperatives in recipes:** *Boil the water. Add a pinch of ajwain. Stir well. Let it cool.*
keyTerms: aromatic — having a pleasant smell
pungent — sharp, strong taste or smell
rhizome — an underground stem, like ginger
imperative — a sentence that gives an instruction

check.q: Ginger and turmeric are actually…
check.why: Both grow as underground stems called rhizomes, though people often call them roots.

sections.h: Let us listen, speak, write and explore
sections.md:
**Listening.** Listen to a short recipe (your teacher may read one, like masala chai). Note the ingredients and the order of steps.

**Speaking — 'Spice of the Day'.** A one-minute talk: name in two languages, where it grows, plant part, taste, one use.

**Speaking — role play.** In pairs, act a scene where a child asks an elder about a spice. Use one *why* question and one *how* question.

**Writing — dialogue.** Write 8–10 lines between you and a grandparent about one spice. Use correct punctuation, two taste adjectives and one question.

**Writing — recipe.** Write a simple recipe (with an adult's help) for jeera water or haldi doodh using imperatives and measure words.

**Explore.** On a map of India, mark where these grow: pepper and cardamom (Kerala, Western Ghats), saffron (Kashmir), turmeric (Telangana, Maharashtra and others), cumin (Gujarat, Rajasthan). Ask: why do different spices grow in different climates?

**Q. Name four spices from the chapter and one use of each.** Turmeric — milk for colds; ginger — tea for cough/nausea; cloves — toothache; cumin — digestion.

**Q. Why do you think the writer chose a conversation format?** It makes information friendly and easy, shows learning between generations, and lets the child ask the questions readers have.

**Q. Why did Europeans want to reach India by sea?** To buy valuable spices such as black pepper directly, without paying middlemen on land routes.

**Q. (Long) 'Our kitchens are our first pharmacies.' Discuss.** Points: list spices and uses; traditional wisdom; scientific support; spice trade history; caution — doctor for serious illness; conclusion on valuing and testing tradition.

sections.md:
For thousands of years Indian spices travelled across seas. Black pepper from the Malabar coast of Kerala was so valued in ancient Rome that it was sometimes called 'black gold'. Arab, Chinese and later European traders sailed to ports like Calicut (Kozhikode) and Muziris. In 1498 the Portuguese sailor **Vasco da Gama** reached Calicut, opening a sea route from Europe — largely in search of spices.

Today India is one of the world's largest producers, consumers and exporters of spices, and Kerala is often called the **Spice Garden of India**.

> **Did you know?** The word *ginger* comes, through Greek and Latin, from an old South Indian word for the root.

sections.h: A spice chart for your notebook
sections.md:
These are **traditional household uses** shared as general knowledge. Spices are foods, not cures — for any illness, see a doctor.

| Spice | Part used | Common traditional use |
|---|---|---|
| Turmeric (haldi) | root (rhizome) | in haldi-doodh; colour to dal and sabzi |
| Ginger (adrak) | root | in tea during colds; in cooking |
| Cumin (jeera) | seed | jeera water after heavy meals |
| Ajwain (carom) | seed | given for stomach discomfort at home |

**Activity:** Visit your kitchen with an adult. Identify five spices by look and smell. Draw each and note which *part of the plant* it comes from — you'll be surprised how many are seeds, barks or buds!

sections.h: Language work: dialogue, -ing words and writing
sections.md:
**Writing a dialogue.** The chapter idea works well as a conversation between a child and a grandparent. Rules: name of speaker, colon, words spoken; no quotation marks needed in play-style dialogue.

> **Meena:** Dadi, why do you add haldi to everything?
> **Dadi:** It gives colour and flavour, and our family has used it for generations.
> **Meena:** Is it medicine, then?
> **Dadi:** It's food. If you are ill, we see the doctor — but good food keeps us strong.

**Grammar — gerunds (-ing as nouns):** *Cooking is fun. Grinding spices takes time. I enjoy smelling cardamom.*

**Sense words:** *aromatic, pungent, tangy, earthy, zesty, warm.*

**Task:** Write a 120-word paragraph: 'My favourite spice and why'. Include where it grows, one dish it goes into, and how it smells and tastes.
keyTerms: aromatic — having a pleasant strong smell
pungent — sharp, strong smell or taste
gerund — an -ing word used as a noun

check.q: In 'Grinding spices takes time', the gerund is…
check.why: Grinding is an -ing verb form acting as the subject noun.

sections.h: A hook: the finish line is ten metres away…
sections.md:
You are running the race of your life. The finish line is just ahead. The runner in front of you has slowed down by mistake — he thinks he has already finished. You could zoom past and win. What do you do?

**Change of Heart** opens Unit 4, *Sports and Wellness*. It is a story about **character change** and **sportsmanship**: the idea that how you play matters as much as whether you win. The 'change of heart' in the title is the turning point when a character's attitude changes — from wanting victory at any cost to choosing fairness, kindness or friendship.

The chapter's text is protected, so we explain it rather than reproduce it. Read it in your Poorvi book (free at ncert.nic.in) and note: *Who competes? What is at stake? What causes the change of heart?* Then use this companion: warm-up, the story's structure, a model story, characters, real-life parallels, themes, wellness (handling winning and losing), grammar (conjunctions), writing a personal narrative, skills activities and exam help.

> **Did you know?** The Olympic motto was expanded in 2021 to 'Faster, Higher, Stronger — Together'. The word *together* was added to stress solidarity.
keyTerms: sportsmanship — fair, generous and respectful behaviour in sport
change of heart — a change in one's feelings or attitude
turning point — the moment that changes the direction of a story

check.q: What does 'a change of heart' mean?
options: a change in one's attitude or feelings
check.why: The phrase means someone's feelings or opinion change, often towards kindness.

sections.md:
**1. Your favourite sport.** Which sport do you play or watch? What does a good player of that sport need — speed, strength, teamwork, patience?

**2. Winning and losing.** Complete: *When I win, I feel… When I lose, I feel…* Is it okay to feel sad after losing? (Yes — what matters is what you do next.)

**3. Fair or unfair?** Discuss: (a) pushing a runner to get ahead; (b) shaking hands after a match; (c) claiming a catch you know you dropped; (d) helping an opponent who is hurt. Sort them.

**4. Predict.** The title is *Change of Heart* and the unit is about sport. Whose heart might change, and why?

check.q: Which is an example of good sportsmanship?
options: Shaking hands with the other team after a match
check.why: Shaking hands shows respect for opponents, whatever the result.

sections.md:
Track the story with this five-step map (fill details from your book):

1. **The goal.** A young athlete wants very badly to win — a race, a match or a tournament. Training, pressure and expectations are described.
2. **The rival.** We meet a competitor. At first the main character sees this person only as an obstacle.
3. **The moment.** During the competition something unexpected happens — the rival falls, gets hurt, makes a mistake, or shows a quality that surprises the main character.
4. **The change of heart.** The main character must choose: grab the advantage, or act fairly and kindly. They choose fairness/kindness.
5. **The result.** Whether or not they win the medal, they win respect — from others and from themselves. The rival may become a friend.

**Before and after.** A character change is easiest to see in a table:

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Wants | the trophy | to do what is right |
| Sees rival as | an obstacle | a fellow person |
| Feels | tense, competitive | calm, proud |

**Why it moves us:** we expect a sports story to end with a trophy. This one ends with something greater: character.

check.q: The 'turning point' of this kind of story is when…
options: the main character chooses fairness over an easy win
check.why: The choice to act kindly is the moment that changes the story's direction — the change of heart.

sections.h: A model story of our own: 'Arya's Race'
sections.md:
*Our own short example of the same pattern — not the textbook story.*

Arya had practised every morning for two months on the dusty school ground in Nagpur. Her elder brother timed her with his phone. The inter-house 400 m trophy was a shining steel cup, and she had already imagined it on the shelf at home.

On Sports Day the whistle blew. Arya took the lead at the first bend. At the second bend she heard a thud behind her. Pooja from the rival house had tripped and was holding her knee on the track.

For three steps Arya kept running. *The cup. The shelf. My brother's face.* Then she heard Pooja trying not to cry. Arya stopped, turned back, and held out her hand. 'Come on. We'll finish together.'

They crossed the line arm in arm, last and second-last. A girl from Green House won the cup. But the whole ground stood up and clapped for the two who came last. That evening the PT teacher gave Arya a small certificate that said *Spirit of Sport*. She put it on the shelf where the cup was meant to go — and decided it looked better there.

**Spot the five steps:** goal (the trophy) → rival (Pooja) → moment (the fall) → change of heart (three steps, then turning back) → result (respect, a certificate, self-respect).

check.q: In 'Arya's Race', what shows the moment of struggle before her change of heart?
options: She keeps running for three steps, thinking of the cup
She sits down at the start
check.why: Those three steps show she was torn between winning and helping before she chose kindness.

sections.md:
Sport history is full of 'change of heart' moments:

- **Navarre, Spain, 2012:** Kenyan runner **Abel Mutai** was leading a cross-country race but slowed down just before the line, thinking he had finished. Spanish runner **Iván Fernández Anaya**, behind him, did not overtake; he signalled and guided Mutai over the line first. He later explained he did not want a victory gained that way.
- **Rio Olympics, 2016:** In a 5,000 m heat, **Nikki Hamblin** (New Zealand) and **Abbey D'Agostino** (USA) collided and fell. They helped each other up and both finished; they received a Fair Play award (the Pierre de Coubertin medal).
- **Cricket:** Players who 'walk' (leave the field without waiting for the umpire when they know they are out) are admired for honesty.

These moments are remembered long after the scores are forgotten.

> **Think about it:** Can you recall a match — school sports day, a gully cricket game — when someone chose fair play?

check.q: In the 2012 race in Spain, what did Iván Fernández Anaya do?
options: He guided the confused leader, Abel Mutai, over the finish line instead of overtaking
check.why: Anaya chose not to profit from Mutai's mistake and helped him finish first.

sections.md:
**1. Sportsmanship over victory.** Winning fairly matters more than winning.

**2. Empathy.** Seeing a rival as a person, not an obstacle.

**3. Integrity.** Doing the right thing even when no rule forces you to.

**4. Inner victory.** Self-respect and respect from others are prizes too.

**5. Wellness.** Unit 4 links sport with wellness: a healthy mind — calm, kind, balanced — is as important as a fit body. Pressure to win at any cost can damage both.

| Win at any cost | Sportsmanship |
|---|---|
| rival = enemy | rival = fellow athlete |
| takes unfair advantage | plays by the spirit of the rules |
| feels empty after a hollow win | feels proud whatever the result |

check.q: 'Integrity' means…
options: doing what is right even when not forced to
check.why: Integrity is honesty and strong moral principles that guide our actions.

sections.md:
Every athlete loses sometimes — even world champions. How we handle feelings is part of being healthy.

**When you lose:**
1. **Name the feeling** — sad, angry, disappointed, embarrassed.
2. **Breathe** — slow breaths (in for 4, out for 4) calm the body.
3. **Talk** — to a friend, parent or coach you trust.
4. **Learn** — write two things that went well and one thing to practise.
5. **Return** — come back to training another day.

**When you win:** celebrate, but thank your team and coach, shake hands, and never mock the losers.

**A balanced athlete** eats well, sleeps 9–11 hours (recommended for children your age), drinks water, warms up before playing and cools down after, and remembers that sport is meant to be fun.

> **Did you know?** Many top athletes work with sports psychologists to manage pressure. Looking after the mind is a strength, not a weakness.

check.q: After losing a match, which is a healthy first step?
options: Name the feeling and breathe slowly
check.why: Recognising the feeling and calming down helps you think clearly and learn from the loss.

sections.h: Let us learn: conjunctions and vocabulary
sections.md:
**Conjunctions join ideas:**
- **because** gives a reason: *She stopped **because** her rival fell.*
- **so** gives a result: *Her rival fell, **so** she stopped.*
- **but** shows contrast: *She wanted the cup, **but** she chose to help.*
- **although** shows an unexpected contrast: ***Although** she lost, she felt proud.*
- **and** adds: *They held hands **and** crossed the line.*

Tip: *because* and *so* are opposites in direction — reason → result with *so*; result ← reason with *because*.

**Sports vocabulary:** *athlete, rival, opponent, track, sprint, finish line, heat (a qualifying race), podium, medal, referee/umpire, fair play.*

**Phrasal verbs from sport:** *give up* (stop trying), *catch up* (reach someone ahead), *keep up* (stay level), *pull through* (succeed despite difficulty), *cheer on* (encourage).

**Feelings in a race:** *nervous, determined, exhausted, torn (unable to decide), proud.*
keyTerms: conjunction — a joining word (because, so, but, although)
phrasal verb — a verb + small word with a special meaning (give up)
rival — a competitor

check.q: Choose the conjunction: '___ Arya lost the race, she felt proud.'
check.why: 'Although' introduces a contrast — losing yet feeling proud.

sections.h: Let us listen, speak, write and explore
sections.md:
**Listening.** Listen to a short sports commentary (radio or your teacher reading). Note the excitement words the commentator uses and how the voice speeds up.

**Speaking — be a commentator.** Give a 30-second live commentary of the moment in the story when the change of heart happens.

**Speaking — discussion.** *'Is it ever right to let an opponent win?'* Share views with reasons.

**Writing — personal narrative (100–120 words): 'The Day I Changed My Mind'.** First person, past tense. Beginning (what you wanted) → event → change → what you learnt. Use two conjunctions.

**Writing — news report (100 words): 'Sports Day: An Act of Fair Play'.** Headline, by-line, date and place; who, what, when, where, why; one quote from a spectator (about a fictional student); close with the lesson.

**Explore.** Find out about the **Arjuna Award** and the **Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna**, India's sports honours. Choose one Indian athlete you admire and write three facts about how they handle pressure.

**Q. What did the main character want at the beginning?** To win the competition at any cost (give details from the book).

**Q. What caused the change of heart?** The unexpected situation involving the rival — describe it.

**Q. What did the character gain, even though they may not have won?** Respect, friendship, self-respect — the true rewards of sport.

**Q. Explain the title.** The story turns on the moment the character's feelings change from competitive to kind.

**Q. (Long) 'True champions are measured by character, not medals.' Discuss using the story and one real-life example.** Use the five-step map plus Mutai–Anaya or Hamblin–D'Agostino.

Themes: sportsmanship, empathy, integrity, inner victory, mental wellness.
Handling a loss: name the feeling, breathe, talk, learn, return.

Useful phrasal verbs: give up, catch up, keep up, pull through, cheer on.

sections.h: How writers show a change of heart
sections.md:
A **change of heart** means a character's feelings or decision turn around. Good writers don't just say *he changed*; they *show* it in three steps:

1. **Before** — the character's goal or attitude (for example, wanting only to win).
2. **The turning point** — something they see, hear or feel that unsettles them: someone hurt, someone kind, a sudden memory.
3. **After** — a new action that proves the change, often costing them something.

When you answer questions, map the character on this **change arc**. Ask: *What did they want? What made them pause? What did they give up?* The bigger the sacrifice, the stronger the change.

> **Did you know?** In the 2016 Rio Olympics, runners Nikki Hamblin and Abbey D'Agostino fell together in a heat; instead of racing on, they helped each other up and finished. Both received a fair-play award.

sections.md:
The unit links sport with wellness of body *and* mind. Sportsmanship includes:
- **Fair play** — following rules even when no one is watching.
- **Respect** — shaking hands, cheering opponents' good shots.
- **Grace** — winning without boasting, losing without sulking.
- **Empathy** — caring when someone is hurt, even a rival.

| Situation | Unsporting | Sporting |
|---|---|---|
| Opponent falls | keep running for the medal | stop and help |
| Umpire's wrong call in your favour | stay silent | tell the truth |
| You lose | blame the pitch | congratulate the winner |

**Discussion:** Is it ever right to give up a win? Give one reason for and one against.
keyTerms: sportsmanship — fair, generous behaviour in games
empathy — feeling with another person
grace — calm, dignified behaviour

check.q: Congratulating the team that beat you shows…
check.why: Respecting the winner is a core part of sportsmanship.

sections.md:
**Idioms about feelings:** *a change of heart* (change of mind or feeling), *heart of gold* (very kind), *lose heart* (become discouraged), *take heart* (feel encouraged), *by heart* (from memory).

**Connectors of contrast:** *but, however, although, yet.* *He wanted the trophy; however, he stopped to help.*

**Writing task — a speech (120 words) for the school sports day: 'Winning with kindness'.** Structure: greeting (*Good morning, respected Principal, teachers and friends*), introduce the topic, two examples, a call to action, thank you.

**Model opening:** *'Good morning, everyone. Today medals will be won and lost, but the moment we will remember is the one when someone chose kindness over the finish line…'*

check.q: 'Don't lose heart' means…
check.why: To lose heart is to lose courage or hope.

Contrast connectors: but, however, although, yet.
A speech has greeting, topic, examples, call to action, thanks.

rd-school-c6-english-b.ch11-the-winner.title: The Winner — It Starts in the Mind
rd-school-c6-english-b.ch11-the-winner.subtitle: A poem about the attitude that turns an ordinary person into a winner

sections.h: A hook: who wins before the race even starts?
sections.md:
Two students stand at the start of a 100 m race. Both trained hard. One thinks, *'I'll probably lose.'* The other thinks, *'I'll give everything I have.'* Coaches will tell you: the second one has a better chance — and even if she loses, she'll grow more.

**The Winner** is the poem in Unit 4, *Sports and Wellness*. Its message is that **winning begins in the mind** — in belief, determination, effort and a refusal to give up. Poems on this theme are often called *inspirational* or *motivational* poems.

The printed poem is protected, so we explain it in our own words. Read it aloud from your Poorvi book (free at ncert.nic.in). This companion covers: warm-up, meaning part by part, what 'winning' really means, qualities of a winner, inspiring Indian examples, poetic devices (including alliteration and contrast), synonyms and antonyms, the first conditional, writing a motivational message, skills activities and exam help.

> **Did you know?** Sports psychologists train athletes in 'self-talk' — the sentences we say to ourselves. Positive self-talk ('I can do this, one step at a time') has been shown to help performance.
keyTerms: attitude — a way of thinking or feeling about something
determination — firmly deciding to do something and sticking to it
self-talk — what we say to ourselves in our minds

check.q: According to the poem's message, winning begins…
options: in the mind — with belief and determination
check.why: The poem stresses that a winner's attitude — belief and effort — comes first.

sections.md:
**1. What is a winner?** Write one sentence: *A winner is someone who…* Compare with a partner. Did either of you mention medals? Did either of you mention trying, improving or helping?

**2. Self-talk check.** Write down three things you sometimes say to yourself before a test or match ('I'm bad at this', 'I'll try my best'). Mark each as *helpful* or *unhelpful*. Rewrite one unhelpful one as helpful.

**3. Picture talk.** Look at a picture of runners at a finish line. Who looks like a 'winner'? Only the one in front?

**4. Predict.** What might a poem called *The Winner* say? Will it be about one race, or about life?

check.q: Which is helpful self-talk before a test?
options: 'I've revised; I'll do one question at a time.'
check.why: Calm, specific, positive self-talk focuses the mind on effort and action.

sections.md:
**1. Thinking decides doing.** The poem suggests that if you believe you are beaten, you already are; if you think you cannot, you won't even try properly.

**2. Effort over excuses.** A winner doesn't wait for perfect conditions. He or she keeps trying even when the odds look poor.

**3. Not always the strongest or fastest.** The poem points out that victory doesn't always go to the biggest or quickest person — but sooner or later, to the one who *believes* and keeps going.

**4. Courage to fail.** Winners accept that falling is part of rising. Each failure is a lesson.

**5. The final idea.** A true 'winner' is someone with a winning spirit — confident, persistent and positive.

**Fair note:** Belief alone isn't magic — you still need practice, rest, good food and coaching. The poem's point is that without belief, even talent goes to waste.

fig.caption: The staircase of a winner: belief, practice, falling, rising again — then victory.
fig.alt: Animated ball climbing steps labelled believe, practise, fall, rise again, win, with a star appearing at the top

check.q: According to the poem, does victory always go to the strongest person?
options: No — it tends to go to the person who believes and keeps trying
check.why: The poem says winning comes from attitude and persistence, not just strength or speed.

sections.md:
The poem widens the meaning of the word *win*.

| Narrow meaning | Wider meaning (the poem's) |
|---|---|
| coming first | doing your personal best |
| a medal or trophy | beating yesterday's you |
| beating others | beating your own fear and laziness |
| one day's result | a lifelong attitude |

**A short example (our own):** Meera finished last in her first swimming race. But for the first time ever, she swam the full length of the pool without stopping. Her coach said, *'You beat yesterday's Meera.'* By the poem's definition, Meera was a winner that day.

**Growth mindset.** Psychologists use this phrase for the belief that abilities grow with effort. Its opposite, a *fixed mindset*, says 'I'm just not good at this'. The poem is a poem of growth mindset. A useful word is **yet**: *I can't do a cartwheel — yet.*

check.q: Which sentence shows a growth mindset?
options: 'I can't bowl a yorker yet, but I'm practising.'
check.why: Adding 'yet' and practising shows the belief that skill grows with effort.

sections.md:
| Quality | What it means | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Self-belief** | trusting your ability | 'I've practised; I'm ready.' |
| **Determination** | sticking to a goal | waking at 5 a.m. to train |
| **Persistence** | not giving up after failure | trying a hard sum five times |
| **Courage** | acting despite fear | volunteering to bowl the last over |
| **Positivity** | expecting good, learning from bad | 'I lost, but I improved my time.' |
| **Humility** | winning without arrogance | shaking hands with the loser |

**Link with 'Change of Heart':** that story showed a winner's *character* (fair play); this poem shows a winner's *mind* (belief and persistence). Together: a true winner is strong inside and kind outside.

**Indian examples of persistence:**
- **M. C. Mary Kom** (boxing) became a world champion several times, including after becoming a mother, and won an Olympic bronze in 2012.
- **Neeraj Chopra** won India's first Olympic gold in athletics — javelin — at the Tokyo Games (held in 2021).
- **Mithali Raj** played international cricket for India for over two decades, one of the longest careers in women's cricket.
- **Arunima Sinha** climbed Mount Everest in 2013 with a prosthetic leg, after losing a leg in a train incident.

check.q: 'Persistence' is best shown by…
check.why: Persistence means keeping on despite failures and difficulties.

sections.md:
**Repetition.** Key words like *think*, *win*, *can* recur, hammering the message home like a coach's chant.

**Conditional lines ('If you think…').** Poems on attitude often use *if… then* lines: *if* you think a certain way, *then* that's what happens.

**Contrast.** winner/loser, strong/weak, can/can't — opposite ideas side by side sharpen the message. Our own example: *'Not the fastest feet but the firmest heart.'*

**Alliteration.** Repeating the same first sound in nearby words makes lines catchy: *brave boys bounce back*; *firm feet, fast finish*. Look for any alliteration in your textbook poem.

**Direct address ('you').** The poem speaks to the reader, so it feels personal.

**Rhyme and rhythm.** A steady beat makes it easy to memorise and recite with energy.

**Tone:** encouraging, confident, energetic.
keyTerms: conditional — an 'if' sentence showing a condition and its result
direct address — speaking straight to the reader as 'you'
alliteration — repeating the first sound in nearby words
contrast — placing opposites side by side

check.q: 'Brave boys bounce back' is an example of…
check.why: The repeated 'b' sound at the start of nearby words is alliteration.

sections.h: Let us learn: synonyms, antonyms and the first conditional
sections.md:
**Synonyms (similar meanings):**
- brave — bold, fearless, courageous
- win — succeed, triumph, prevail
- try — attempt, strive, endeavour
- strong — powerful, sturdy, tough

**Antonyms (opposite meanings):**
- brave ↔ cowardly, timid
- win ↔ lose
- strong ↔ weak
- confident ↔ doubtful
- success ↔ failure

**Word ladder** (from weak to strong meaning): *try → strive → fight hard*; *good → great → outstanding*.

**First conditional:** *If + present simple, will + verb.*
- *If you **practise** daily, you **will** improve.*
- *If she **believes** in herself, she **will** try harder.*
- *If we **give up** now, we **won't** know how far we could go.*
Common mistake: *If you will practise…* ✗ — don't use *will* in the *if* part.

check.q: Which is correct?
options: If you will train, you win.
If you train, you will win.
If you trained, you will win.
check.why: First conditional: present simple in the 'if' clause, 'will + verb' in the result.

sections.h: Let us listen, speak, write and explore
sections.md:
**Listening.** Listen to a short motivational talk or an interview with an athlete. Note one sentence of advice and one story of failure turned into success.

**Speaking — recitation.** Recite the poem with energy; stress words like *win* and *can*; finish strongly. Try reciting it once slowly and once like a coach's chant — which suits it better?

**Speaking — 'My hero' talk.** One minute on a sportsperson you admire: who, sport, one difficulty they overcame, one quality from the table.

**Writing — a motivational message (40–60 words).** For a classmate before Sports Day or exams. Address them by name, give encouragement, include one piece of practical advice and end with a short punchy line. Example close: *Run your race, not theirs!*

**Writing — a short speech** for the Sports Day assembly on *'Everyone can be a winner'*.

**Explore.** Make a class 'Wall of Winners' — each student writes one thing they achieved through persistence (learning to cycle, a song, a difficult sum).

sections.md:
**Q. What is the central idea of the poem?** Winning starts with a positive, determined mind; belief and effort lead to success.

**Q. Who is a 'winner' according to the poet?** Someone who believes in himself/herself, keeps trying and doesn't let fear or failure stop them.

**Q. Why does the poet address the reader as 'you'?** To make the message personal and direct, like a coach speaking to each reader.

**Q. (Long) 'Whether you think you can or you can't, you're usually right.' Explain with reference to the poem.** Discuss self-belief, effort, examples (exam prep, sport), growth mindset, balance (belief + practice), conclusion.

sections.h: The poem's big idea in four moves
sections.md:
The poem's message can be traced through four steps, each building on the last:

1. **Thought comes first.** If you already believe you will fail, you probably won't try your best — so the defeat begins in your head.
2. **Daring matters.** Wanting to win is not enough; you must be willing to attempt, to risk looking silly.
3. **Confidence grows from belief.** Thinking 'I can' raises your effort and focus.
4. **The real prize-winner.** Victory does not always go to the strongest or fastest, but to the one who keeps believing and keeps working.

Notice the poem's balance: it never says belief alone wins — it says belief *starts* the effort that wins. Use this nuance in long answers.

> **Did you know?** Psychologists call this a **growth mindset** (a term made popular by Carol Dweck): the belief that ability grows with practice. Students taught this idea often try harder problems.

sections.md:
- **Repetition of 'if you think…'** — each stanza opens with a condition, so the poem sounds like advice from a coach.
- **Antithesis (contrast):** *win / lose, strong / weak, beaten / winner* — opposites placed side by side make the message sharp.
- **Rhyming couplets:** pairs of lines rhyme, which makes the poem easy to memorise — like a motivational chant.
- **Second person 'you':** the poet speaks directly to the reader, so it feels personal.

**Language note:** *conditional sentences* — *If you think you can, you will try.* Structure: **If + present, will + verb.** Write three of your own about sport or study.

sections.h: A hook: the world's biggest exercise class
sections.md:
Every year on **21 June** — the longest day in the Northern Hemisphere — millions of people across the world unroll mats in parks, beaches, schools and even on navy ships. It is **International Day of Yoga**, declared by the United Nations General Assembly in **December 2014** after India proposed it; the first was held in **2015**.

**Yoga — A Way of Life** is an informative (non-fiction) chapter in Unit 4, *Sports and Wellness*. It explains what yoga is, where it comes from, its main parts — postures, breathing, meditation, good conduct — and how it helps both body and mind.

The chapter's own text is protected, so this companion explains the same topics in the same order in our own words: warm-up → features of the text → meaning and origin → the eight limbs → asanas, Surya Namaskar and pranayama → benefits → a daily routine and safety → language (imperatives, sequence words) → skills activities → exam help. Read the chapter in your Poorvi book too (free at ncert.nic.in).

> **Did you know?** The word *yoga* comes from the Sanskrit root *yuj*, meaning 'to join' or 'to unite' — uniting body, breath and mind.
keyTerms: yoga — from Sanskrit 'yuj', to join; a discipline uniting body and mind
non-fiction — writing based on facts
International Day of Yoga — 21 June

check.q: The Sanskrit root 'yuj' means…
check.why: Yoga comes from 'yuj', meaning to unite — joining body, breath and mind.

sections.md:
**1. What do you know?** Make a K-W-L chart: **K**now (what you already know about yoga), **W**ant to know, **L**earnt (fill at the end).

**2. Body check.** Sit still for one minute with your eyes closed. Notice your breath. Is it fast or slow? Where do you feel it — chest or belly? Share how you felt afterwards.

**3. Screens and posture.** How many hours a day do you sit bent over books, phones or screens? What might that do to your back and neck?

**4. Poses you know.** Can anyone in the class show a pose (safely)? Name it in Sanskrit or English if you can.

check.why: K-W-L = what I Know, what I Want to know, what I Learnt.

sections.md:
This chapter is different from the stories and poems earlier in the book. Look out for these **features of informative writing**:

- **Headings and sub-headings** that divide the topic (meaning, history, types, benefits).
- **Facts and dates** (21 June, the UN declaration).
- **Technical words** — often Sanskrit — with explanations: *asana, pranayama, dhyana*.
- **Pictures or diagrams** of poses with labels.
- **Instructions** in short imperative sentences: *Stand straight. Breathe in.*
- **A neutral, explaining tone** — the writer informs rather than tells a story.

**Reading strategy — skim and scan.** *Skim* first: read headings and first lines to get the big picture. Then *scan*: look quickly for a specific fact (e.g., 'Who compiled the Yoga Sutras?').

**Fact or opinion?** *Yoga began in ancient India* — fact. *Yoga is the best exercise in the world* — opinion. Non-fiction should be mostly facts; notice when a writer gives an opinion.

check.q: Which sentence is an opinion?
options: International Day of Yoga is on 21 June.
Yoga is the most enjoyable activity ever.
check.why: 'Most enjoyable ever' is a personal judgement, not a checkable fact.

sections.h: Origins: a very old Indian tradition
sections.md:
- Yoga developed in ancient India over thousands of years. Some scholars point to seals from the **Harappan civilisation** showing a figure in a seated posture as a possible early sign, though historians debate what the figure means.
- Ideas of meditation and self-discipline appear in the **Upanishads** and the **Bhagavad Gita**.
- The sage **Patanjali** compiled the **Yoga Sutras** (usually dated roughly 2,000 years ago; scholars give different dates), which organise yoga into a clear system.
- Later traditions, such as **Hatha Yoga**, developed many physical postures.
- In the 20th century, teachers carried yoga around the world; today it is practised in almost every country.

**Yoga is not just exercise.** It is a *way of life* — about how you eat, sleep, behave, breathe and think.

Philosophy of self-control and meditation
Patanjali's Yoga Sutras (dates debated)
Hatha Yoga texts describe postures and breathing

First International Day of Yoga
UNESCO lists yoga as Intangible Cultural Heritage

fig.caption: Yoga's long journey from ancient India to the whole world.

check.q: Who compiled the Yoga Sutras?
check.why: The sage Patanjali is credited with compiling the Yoga Sutras, which systematised yoga.

sections.md:
Patanjali described yoga as having **eight limbs** (*ashta* = eight, *anga* = limb):

| # | Limb | Simple meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Yama** | good behaviour towards others (non-violence, truthfulness, not stealing…) |
| 2 | **Niyama** | good habits for oneself (cleanliness, contentment, self-study…) |
| 3 | **Asana** | steady, comfortable postures |
| 4 | **Pranayama** | control and regulation of breath |
| 5 | **Pratyahara** | turning the senses inward, away from distractions |
| 6 | **Dharana** | concentration on one point |
| 7 | **Dhyana** | meditation — continuous calm focus |
| 8 | **Samadhi** | complete absorption, deep peace |

Notice: postures are just *one* of eight! The first two are about **values and character** — which is why the chapter calls yoga *a way of life*.

**Memory trick:** *Your Nice Aunt Prepares Pakoras During Diwali Season* — Y N A P P D D S.

check.q: Which limb of yoga is about controlling the breath?
check.why: Pranayama ('prana' life-breath + 'ayama' control/extension) is regulated breathing.

sections.h: Asanas and breathing you may know
sections.md:
| Asana | Looks like | Helps (generally) |
|---|---|---|
| **Tadasana** (mountain) | standing tall, arms up | posture, balance |
| **Vrikshasana** (tree) | standing on one leg, foot on inner thigh, palms joined | balance, concentration |
| **Bhujangasana** (cobra) | lying face down, lifting chest | flexible back |
| **Padmasana** (lotus) | seated, cross-legged, feet on thighs | steady sitting for breathing/meditation |
| **Shavasana** (corpse) | lying flat, fully relaxed | rest and relaxation |
| **Surya Namaskar** | a flowing sequence of 12 steps | whole-body warm-up |

**Breathing:** *Anulom-vilom* (alternate-nostril breathing) and slow deep belly breathing calm the mind. Long, slow out-breaths help the body relax.

**Safety first:**
- Learn from a trained teacher.
- Practise on an empty or light stomach, on a mat.
- Never force a pose; stop if anything hurts.
- If you have a health condition, check with your doctor first.

sections.md:
*Surya Namaskar* (Sun Salutation) links twelve positions in a smooth flow with the breath. Learn it from a teacher; this list is to help you remember the order.

| Step | Position | Breath |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Pranamasana — stand, palms joined at chest | breathe out |
| 2 | Hasta Uttanasana — raise arms, bend back gently | breathe in |
| 3 | Padahastasana — bend forward, hands towards feet | breathe out |
| 4 | Ashwa Sanchalanasana — one leg back, look up | breathe in |
| 5 | Dandasana — plank, body straight | hold / breathe out |
| 6 | Ashtanga Namaskara — knees, chest, chin to floor | hold |
| 7 | Bhujangasana — cobra, chest up | breathe in |
| 8 | Adho Mukha Svanasana — hips up, inverted V | breathe out |
| 9 | Ashwa Sanchalanasana — other leg forward | breathe in |
| 10 | Padahastasana — forward bend | breathe out |
| 11 | Hasta Uttanasana — arms up | breathe in |
| 12 | Tadasana/Pranamasana — stand, relax | breathe out |

(Different schools name or order a few steps slightly differently.) Notice the pattern: **bending back or opening = breathe in; bending forward or folding = breathe out.**

check.q: In Surya Namaskar, bending forward usually goes with…
check.why: Folding forward compresses the belly, so we breathe out; opening up goes with breathing in.

sections.md:
**Body**
- improves **flexibility** and **balance**
- builds **strength** and better **posture** (great for students bent over desks and phones!)
- supports healthy breathing

**Mind**
- reduces **stress** and calms nerves before exams or matches
- improves **concentration** and memory
- helps **sleep**

**Character and life**
- self-discipline (regular practice)
- kindness and honesty (yama/niyama)
- awareness of one's body and feelings

**Why it suits everyone:** no costly equipment, any age can start (with suitable poses), can be done at home.

**Try it — a 2-minute calm-down (safe for everyone):** sit tall; close your eyes; breathe in through the nose for 4 counts; breathe out slowly for 6 counts; repeat 8 times; notice how your shoulders drop. Use it before a test or after a quarrel.

> **Did you know?** In 2016 UNESCO added *Yoga* to its list of the **Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity**.

check.q: Which is a MENTAL benefit of yoga?
check.why: Breathing and meditation in yoga help calm the mind and improve focus.

sections.h: Let us learn: instructions, imperatives and sequence words
sections.md:
**Imperatives (instructions):** *Stand straight. Breathe in slowly. Raise your arms. Hold for five seconds. Relax.* Instructional writing uses short imperative sentences (the verb comes first, the subject *you* is understood) and **sequence words**: *first, next, then, after that, finally.*

**Worked example — steps for Vrikshasana (tree pose):**
1. **First**, stand tall with your feet together and arms by your sides.
2. **Next**, shift your weight onto your left foot.
3. **Then** place the sole of your right foot on the inside of your left thigh (or calf — never on the knee).
4. Join your palms in front of your chest; fix your eyes on one point.
5. **After that**, breathe in and raise your joined hands above your head. Hold for a few slow breaths.
6. **Finally**, lower your arms and foot slowly and repeat on the other side.

**Negative imperatives** for safety: *Don't force the pose. Don't hold your breath.*

**Sanskrit words in English:** *asana, pranayama, dhyana, namaskar* — written in italics or explained the first time.
keyTerms: imperative — a sentence that gives an instruction
sequence words — first, next, then, finally
skim — read quickly for the main idea
scan — look quickly for a specific fact

check.q: Which sentence is an imperative?
check.why: 'Breathe in slowly' gives an instruction with the verb first.

sections.h: Let us listen, speak, write and explore
sections.md:
**Listening.** Your teacher gives spoken instructions for a simple pose. Follow them, then discuss: which words told you the *order*?

**Speaking — be the instructor.** In pairs, guide your partner through Tadasana using five imperatives and two sequence words.

**Speaking — assembly speech:** *'Yoga for Students'* — greeting; meaning; brief history; two asanas; benefits (study stress, posture, focus); safety; appeal to practise daily; thanks.

**Writing — a poster** for International Day of Yoga at your school: date, time, venue, three benefits, a slogan.

**Writing — a routine.** Plan a 15-minute morning routine: 2 min warm-up, 5 min Surya Namaskar (with a teacher's guidance), 5 min asanas, 3 min breathing and Shavasana.

**Explore.** Ask grandparents whether they practised yoga, pranayama or walking in their youth. Compare with your habits. Also find out about one other Indian wellness tradition — such as *kalaripayattu* from Kerala or *mallakhamb* from Maharashtra.

**Q. What does 'yoga' mean?** It comes from Sanskrit *yuj* — to join/unite body, mind and breath.

**Q. Why is yoga called 'a way of life'?** Because it includes values (yama, niyama), habits, breathing and meditation, not only exercise.

**Q. When is International Day of Yoga and why that date?** 21 June, the longest day in the Northern Hemisphere; declared by the UN in 2014, first held in 2015.

**Q. Name the eight limbs.** Yama, niyama, asana, pranayama, pratyahara, dharana, dhyana, samadhi.

**Q. (Long) Write a speech for the school assembly on 'Yoga for Students'.** Follow the plan in the speaking section; use at least one fact, one example and one appeal.
